title: What is the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ)?
dek: The Committee to Protect Journalists is a New York non-profit, founded in 1981, that documents journalists killed and jailed. Who runs it and who funds it.
body_md:
The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) is an independent non-profit organization, founded in 1981 and based in New York, that documents journalists killed, imprisoned and threatened around the world and advocates for them ([glossary](/glossary/committee-to-protect-journalists); [FAQ](https://cpj.org/about/faq/)). CPJ says it is funded by individuals, corporations and foundations, does not accept government funding, and is led by its chief executive, Jodie Ginsberg ([FAQ](https://cpj.org/about/faq/); [staff list](https://cpj.org/about/staff/)).

## Who is the Committee to Protect Journalists?

CPJ describes itself as "an independent, nonprofit organization founded in 1981" that "promotes press freedom worldwide by defending the rights of journalists to report the news without fear of reprisal" ([FAQ](https://cpj.org/about/faq/)). Its mission statement reads: "The Committee to Protect Journalists promotes press freedom worldwide and defends the right of journalists to report the news safely and without fear of reprisal" ([about page](https://cpj.org/about/)).

"In 1981, a group of U.S. foreign correspondents created CPJ," according to the organization ([FAQ](https://cpj.org/about/faq/)). It has headquarters in New York, an office in Washington, D.C., and representatives in cities including Bangkok, Beirut, Istanbul, Mexico City and Nairobi, and "a board of prominent journalists directs CPJ's activities."

## Who is the CEO of the Committee to Protect Journalists?

Jodie Ginsberg is chief executive officer. She joined CPJ in 2022 from Internews Europe, where she was chief executive, after a career at the Reuters news agency and six years leading a London-based freedom of expression group ([staff list](https://cpj.org/about/staff/)).

## Who funds the Committee to Protect Journalists?

"CPJ is funded solely by contributions from individuals, corporations, and foundations. CPJ does not accept government funding," the organization states ([FAQ](https://cpj.org/about/faq/)). It publishes its United States tax filings (Form 990) and audited financial statements ([financial statements](https://cpj.org/about/financial-statements/)).

## What does CPJ do?

CPJ's stated reason for its work is that "without a free press, few other human rights are attainable" ([FAQ](https://cpj.org/about/faq/)). CPJ counted 132 journalists and media workers killed in 2025 and 336 imprisoned as of December 1, 2025, and says it gave training or emergency assistance to 2,300 journalists in 2025 ([about page](https://cpj.org/about/)). It says it works in "more than 120 countries" and that each case it classifies "is corroborated by more than one source for factual accuracy" ([FAQ](https://cpj.org/about/faq/)). In 2013 it published a report on Espionage Act prosecutions of sources in the United States ([record](/incidents/2013-obama-doj-charges-eight-under-espionage-act)).

## What has CPJ said about the White House ban?

On September 18, 2026, CPJ said the order to ban news outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House news coverage "violates First Amendment rights and is an alarming escalation of how far this administration will go to control the narrative and silence critical, fact-based, news coverage" ([statement, 2026-09-18](https://cpj.org/2026/09/cpj-president-trumps-arbitrary-cnn-ms-now-politico-ban-violates-first-amendment-rights/); [record](/incidents/2026-white-house-bans-cnn-msnow-politico)).

On September 21, 2026, leading news organizations, including the Associated Press, The New York Times and The Washington Post, joined a CPJ statement saying the ban "sets a dangerous precedent, one in which the President decides what the American people can know" ([statement, 2026-09-21](https://cpj.org/2026/09/leading-news-outlets-issue-statement-in-defense-of-a-us-free-press/)). Ginsberg said: "Enough is enough."

## What does CPJ report outside the United States?

On September 22, 2026, CPJ wrote that "as Serbians prepare to vote in October parliamentary elections, journalists covering the polls are at serious risk of threats, violence and hostility of the sort that has become increasingly common during President Aleksandar Vučić's time in office" ([report, 2026-09-22](https://cpj.org/2026/09/assaulted-and-threatened-risks-surge-for-journalists-ahead-of-serbia-elections/)). It had documented at least 28 Serbian journalists reporting being struck, detained or sprayed with chemical irritants by police between June and September 2025 ([record](/incidents/2025-serbia-police-target-journalists-protests)).

## What other organizations protect journalists?

Others include [Reporters Without Borders (RSF)](/glossary/reporters-without-borders) in Paris, the [Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press](/glossary/reporters-committee-for-freedom-of-the-press) and the [Freedom of the Press Foundation](/glossary/freedom-of-the-press-foundation), which runs the [U.S. Press Freedom Tracker](/glossary/us-press-freedom-tracker).

title: Sherrill v. Knight: the 1977 ruling on White House press passes
dek: Sherrill v. Knight (D.C. Cir. 1977) held that a White House press pass may not be denied arbitrarily and requires notice, a reply and written reasons.
body_md:
Sherrill v. Knight is a 1977 decision of the United States Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit holding that once the White House opens press facilities to journalists, a White House press pass may not be denied "arbitrarily or for less than compelling reasons" ([opinion, 569 F.2d 124](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)). The court required "notice of the factual bases for denial, an opportunity for the applicant to respond to these, and a final written statement of the reasons for denial," and courts in Washington have applied that rule to press pass disputes since ([case record](/cases/sherrill-v-knight-1977)).

## What was Sherrill v. Knight about?

Robert Sherrill had been Washington correspondent for The Nation, a weekly magazine, since 1965, and held credentials for the House and Senate press galleries of the United States Congress, the national legislature ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)). In 1966 he applied for a White House press pass and was refused ([case record](/cases/sherrill-v-knight-1977)). The White House is the office and residence of the president of the United States in Washington, D.C.

The refusal came from the [Secret Service](/glossary/secret-service), the federal agency that protects the president. The opinion states that "the denial resulted solely from the determination of the Secret Service, after investigating Mr. Sherrill, that he not be issued the pass" ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)). A Secret Service memorandum to Bill Moyers, then White House press secretary, dated May 3, 1966, asked that the background information behind the decision "not be disclosed to Mr. Sherrill or his employer" ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)). H. Stuart Knight, the named defendant, was director of the United States Secret Service when the case reached the appeals court ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)).

### How White House press passes were issued in the 1970s

The court found that "there exist no written procedures pertaining to the issuance of press passes for the White House" ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)). A journalist applied to the White House Press Office, which checked that the applicant held House and Senate press gallery passes, lived in the Washington area and needed to report from the White House regularly. The press office forwards the application "to the Secret Service for a security check, including a background FBI investigation," and "whether a pass is then issued depends solely on the recommendation of the Secret Service" ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)).

Applicants who were refused were told, orally or in writing, that the denial was "for reasons relating to the security of the President and/or the members of his immediate family." When Sherrill asked why he had been refused, "Secret Service personnel replied that 'we can't tell you the reasons'" ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)). He reapplied for a press credential in January 1972 and was refused again ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)).

### How Sherrill learned the reason

Also in January 1972, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), a United States civil liberties organization, requested Press Secretary Ziegler (Ronald Ziegler) to state in writing whether Sherrill had been denied a pass and why ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)). Sherrill had never received written notice thereof. A letter signed on February 11, 1972, stated that he had been denied accreditation "for reasons of security" on May 3, 1966 ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)).

The ACLU then filed a request under the [Freedom of Information Act (FOIA)](/glossary/foia), the 1966 United States law that gives the public a right to request federal records. The Secret Service advised that the material was exempt. On June 26, 1972, Eugene Rossides, an assistant secretary of the Treasury, denied the appeal but wrote: "For Mr. Sherrill's information, he has been arrested and fined for physical assault in the State of Florida" ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)). The court called this "the first and only indication Mr. Sherrill received of the reason he was considered a security risk." A footnote records that the Secret Service decision also rested on "a 1962 assault charge in Texas" and on an allegation that Sherrill was "mentally unbalanced" ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)).

A second journalist, Thomas Forcade, denied a White House press pass in 1971, joined the suit and later withdrew ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)).

## What did the district court decide?

Sherrill sued in the [United States District Court for the District of Columbia](/glossary/us-district-court-dc), the federal trial court in Washington, D.C., alleging that the denial under the foregoing circumstances violated the first and fifth amendments to the Constitution ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)). The [First Amendment](/glossary/first-amendment) protects freedom of speech and of the press, and the [Fifth Amendment](/glossary/fifth-amendment) guarantees [due process](/glossary/due-process), fair procedure before the government takes away a person's liberty or property.

In Forcade v. Knight, 416 F.Supp. 1025 (D.D.C. 1976), the district court did not order a pass issued. It told the Secret Service to "devise and publicize narrow and specific standards" for press pass denials, to give applicants notice of the evidence, to let them rebut it, and to issue a final written decision ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)). The district court based the written-decision requirement on its view that denying a pass to a bona fide journalist violates the First Amendment unless it furthers a compelling governmental interest identified by narrowly drawn standards; without a written decision, it said, it could not undertake proper judicial review. On notice and rebuttal, the court relied on a finding that a denial deprives a journalist of "liberty" under the Fifth Amendment. The government appealed.

## What did the D.C. Circuit hold?

The [D.C. Circuit](/glossary/dc-circuit), the federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., heard argument on September 23, 1977, and decided the case on December 15, 1977. Judges Carl McGowan, Harold Leventhal and Roger Robb sat on the panel, and McGowan wrote the opinion ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)).

The government argued that because the public has no First Amendment right of access to the White House, and the press has no greater right than the public, a denial violates the First Amendment only if it is based on the content of the journalist's speech ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)). The court agreed that "arbitrary or content-based criteria for press pass issuance are prohibited under the first amendment," but found further First Amendment interests at stake.

The court wrote that "the White House has voluntarily decided to establish press facilities for correspondents who need to report therefrom." With White House press facilities open to the press, the protection afforded newsgathering under the First Amendment guarantee "requires that this access not be denied arbitrarily or for less than compelling reasons" ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)). It added that "the public at large" also has an interest "in assuring that restrictions on newsgathering be no more arduous than necessary, and that individual newsmen not be arbitrarily excluded from sources of information."

### The standard: physical danger to the president

The court accepted that protecting the president is a compelling governmental interest, and that Sherrill's denial "proceeded solely from concern for 'the physical security of the President'" ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)). It called the phrase "reasons of security" "unnecessarily vague and subject to ambiguous interpretation" and required the Secret Service to "publish or otherwise make publicly known the actual standard." It did not require the narrow and specific standards the district court had ordered. It was enough, the court held, that the Secret Service be guided "solely by the principle of whether the applicant presents a potential source of physical danger to the President and/or his immediate family so serious as to justify his exclusion" ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)). That standard, it said, allowed meaningful judicial review, and reviewing courts would be "appropriately deferential" to the Secret Service.

### The procedure: notice, reply, written reasons

The court held that "notice of the factual bases for denial, an opportunity for the applicant to respond to these, and a final written statement of the reasons for denial are compelled" because a bona fide Washington correspondent's interest in a pass is protected by the First Amendment, and that interest "undoubtedly qualifies as liberty which may not be denied without due process of law under the fifth amendment" ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)). The final written statement, it said, would show that the agency had not relied on "additional, undisclosed information" and would prevent a repeat of Sherrill's case, where official written notification came "more than five years after the status decision is made." The court affirmed the procedural part of the judgment and sent the standards part back to be modified to fit the First Amendment analysis ([case record](/cases/sherrill-v-knight-1977)). The site's glossary summarizes the result as the [Sherrill v. Knight standard](/glossary/sherrill-v-knight-standard).

### What Sherrill v. Knight did not decide

The court said the case did not concern the general public's entry to the White House, and did not challenge "the discretion of the President to grant interviews or briefings with selected journalists" ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)). Sherrill's First Amendment claim was not that "the White House must open its doors to the press, conduct press conferences, or operate press facilities." In a footnote, the court said it had no occasion to consider "what procedures must be employed in the revocation, for security reasons, of an already-issued White House press pass" ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)).

## How have courts used Sherrill v. Knight since 1977?

The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press (RCFP), a United States non-profit that gives legal help to journalists, filed a brief in Sherrill v. Knight with the White House Correspondents' Association, the organization of reporters who cover the president, and the National Press Club ([RCFP](https://www.rcfp.org/karem-dc-circuit-press-pass-ruling/)).

On November 7, 2018, the White House suspended the [hard pass](/glossary/hard-pass), the standing credential for White House entry, of CNN correspondent Jim Acosta after a news conference with President Donald Trump ([record](/incidents/2018-white-house-revokes-acosta-press-pass)). On November 16, 2018, Judge Timothy J. Kelly granted CNN a temporary restraining order "on due process grounds drawn from Sherrill v. Knight," and the White House restored the pass on November 19 ([case record](/cases/cnn-v-trump-2018); [Yahoo News / AP](https://news.yahoo.com/white-house-restores-jim-acosta-212020316.html)).

In June 2020, in Brian Karem's case, a D.C. Circuit panel held that the White House could not suspend a Playboy correspondent's pass on "unarticulated standards of professionalism." Judge David S. Tatel wrote: "Forty years on, today's hard-pass system is little changed from the one described in Sherrill" ([RCFP](https://www.rcfp.org/karem-dc-circuit-press-pass-ruling/)).

In 2025, the Associated Press (AP) case turned on a different question: access to the Oval Office, the president's office, and other small spaces. On June 6, 2025, a D.C. Circuit panel allowed the White House, 2 to 1, to keep the AP out of those spaces; Judge Neomi Rao wrote that "these restricted presidential spaces are not First Amendment fora opened for private speech and discussion" ([CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2025/06/06/politics/white-house-ban-associated-press-continue); [case record](/cases/ap-v-budowich-2025)).

The record lists Sherrill v. Knight as precedent for the September 2026 deactivation of hard passes held by CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters, which the three outlets challenged in Cable News Network, Inc. v. Trump, No. 1:26-cv-03287, pending as of September 22, 2026 ([record](/incidents/2026-white-house-bans-cnn-msnow-politico); [case record](/cases/cnn-msnow-politico-v-trump-2026)).

### Sherrill v. Knight timeline, 1965 to 2026

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 1965 | Sherrill becomes Washington correspondent for The Nation |
| 1966-05-03 | Secret Service tells the press secretary Sherrill will not be issued a pass |
| 1972-01 | Sherrill reapplies and is refused; ACLU asks for reasons |
| 1972-06-26 | Treasury letter cites a Florida arrest and fine |
| 1976 | District court orders standards and procedures (Forcade v. Knight) |
| 1977-12-15 | D.C. Circuit affirms procedures, modifies standards ([case](/cases/sherrill-v-knight-1977)) |
| 2018-11-16 | Acosta order relies on Sherrill ([case](/cases/cnn-v-trump-2018)) |
| 2020-06 | Karem ruling cites Sherrill ([RCFP](https://www.rcfp.org/karem-dc-circuit-press-pass-ruling/)) |
| 2026-09-21 | CNN, MS NOW and Politico sue ([case](/cases/cnn-msnow-politico-v-trump-2026)) |

Sources for the table: the [opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json) (1965 to 1977) and the linked record pages.

## Do other countries review refusals of press credentials?

The record files refusals of press credentials under [credential control](/tactics/credential_control). In Türkiye, the Council of State, the highest administrative court, suspended rules that let the presidency deny or cancel press cards, finding the grounds too broad ([record](/incidents/2021-turkiye-press-card-controls-restrictive)).

title: What is the White House press pool?
dek: The White House press pool is the small rotating group of reporters who cover the US president in tight spaces. Who picks it, who pays, what changed.
body_md:
The White House press pool is a small, rotating group of reporters, photographers and television and radio crews who cover the president of the United States in places too small for the whole press corps, such as the Oval Office, the president's office, and Air Force One, the president's aircraft, and who share what they gather with every other outlet ([glossary: press pool](/glossary/press-pool)). For more than a century the White House Correspondents' Association chose which outlets rotated into the pool, and since February 25, 2025, the White House has made that choice itself ([record](/incidents/2025-whca-loses-control-of-press-pool)).

## What is the White House press pool, and who is in it?

The White House is the office and residence of the president of the United States in Washington, D.C. On the White House grounds, the pool is "typically a group of 20 correspondents from wire services, print outlets, TV and radio, along with photojournalists and sound operators," according to the [White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA)](https://whca.press/covering-the-white-house/), the organization of reporters who cover the president ([glossary: WHCA](/glossary/whca)).

Of the pool members, the print reporter on duty writes a [pool report](/glossary/pool-report), which is emailed to the full press corps and to a longer list kept by the White House Press Office, the president's communications staff ([WHCA](https://whca.press/covering-the-white-house/)). The TV crew, the radio correspondent and still photographers share video, audio and pictures the same way, so that other media outlets not in the room can report the same facts ([AP via MPR News](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/09/22/what-is-the-white-house-pool-its-a-battleground-between-trump-and-free-press-rights)).

For print reporters, the WHCA wrote that "roughly 32 print outlets serve in this in-town pool, so each gets a turn about once a month," and that "AP, Bloomberg and Reuters have permanent slots in the pool" ([WHCA](https://whca.press/covering-the-white-house/)). That description predates April 15, 2025, when the White House ended the wire services' guaranteed seat (see the table below).

## Who pays for pool coverage?

The news outlets pay. The WHCA calls daily coverage of the president "a solemn obligation that news organizations undertake at their own expense" ([WHCA](https://whca.press/covering-the-white-house/)). According to Reporters Without Borders (RSF), a press freedom organization based in Paris, the television pool is "an arrangement among ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC, and Fox News to take turns covering presidential events, intended to spread the financial and logistical burden among the five stations" ([RSF, 2026-09-22](https://rsf.org/en/usa-white-house-media-ban-robs-public-access-independent-presidential-coverage)). The five networks supply the live coverage and footage that other media outlets use.

Pool duty, the WHCA says, "requires 13 journalists to be on assignment" from call time to the "lid," the notice from aides that the president will not appear in public again that day ([WHCA](https://whca.press/covering-the-white-house/)).

## Why does the press pool matter?

Pool reporters covering the president have travelled with presidents since Franklin Roosevelt, president of the United States from 1933 to 1945; three wire service reporters were with him at Warm Springs, Georgia, when he died in 1945, according to the [WHCA](https://whca.press/covering-the-white-house/). The pool was in President John F. Kennedy's motorcade in Dallas on November 22, 1963, when he was assassinated ([AP via MPR News](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/09/22/what-is-the-white-house-pool-its-a-battleground-between-trump-and-free-press-rights)).

The WHCA's stated rationale is that "the American public must never come to depend on a president's aides alone to provide the world with information on his activities" ([WHCA](https://whca.press/covering-the-white-house/)).

## Who controls the White House press pool now?

On February 11, 2025, the Trump administration began excluding Associated Press (AP) journalists from the Oval Office and Air Force One after the AP kept the name "Gulf of Mexico" in its style guide ([record](/incidents/2025-white-house-bars-ap-gulf-of-america)). President Donald Trump said, "We're going to keep them out until such time as they agree that it's the Gulf of America," according to [NPR](https://www.npr.org/2025/02/21/nx-s1-5305226/ap-sues-white-house-gulf-of-america-mexico-trump).

On February 25, 2025, the White House announced that it would select the pool itself. The WHCA said the change "suggests the government will choose the journalists who cover the president" ([WHCA statement](https://whca.press/2025/02/25/whca-statement-on-white-house-announcement-on-press-pool/); [record](/incidents/2025-whca-loses-control-of-press-pool)). As of September 22, 2026, "the White House now picks and chooses which members of the media make up the pool," according to the [AP](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/09/22/what-is-the-white-house-pool-its-a-battleground-between-trump-and-free-press-rights).

The AP sued. On June 6, 2025, a panel of the D.C. Circuit, the federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., allowed the exclusion to continue for the Oval Office, Air Force One, Mar-a-Lago and the Cabinet Room, by 2 to 1 ([case record](/cases/ap-v-budowich-2025)). Judge Neomi Rao wrote that "these restricted presidential spaces are not First Amendment fora opened for private speech and discussion" ([CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2025/06/06/politics/white-house-ban-associated-press-continue)).

### Pool changes, 2025 to 2026

| Date | Action | Status as of 2026-09-22 |
|---|---|---|
| 2025-02-11 | AP excluded from Oval Office and Air Force One ([record](/incidents/2025-white-house-bars-ap-gulf-of-america)) | Partly in effect; on appeal |
| 2025-02-25 | White House takes over pool selection from the WHCA ([record](/incidents/2025-whca-loses-control-of-press-pool)) | In effect |
| 2025-04-15 | Wire services lose their guaranteed daily seat ([record](/incidents/2025-white-house-cuts-wire-service-pool-slot)) | In effect |
| 2026-09-19 | Hard passes of CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters deactivated ([record](/incidents/2026-white-house-bans-cnn-msnow-politico)) | In effect; case pending |
| 2026-09-20 | Other TV networks decline to replace CNN's pool crew ([AP via Action News Now](https://www.actionnewsnow.com/news/major-tv-networks-stand-with-cnn-decline-to-replace-its-white-house-pool-crew/article_47bdc4b7-11bd-5c5a-a581-dabefc858a0b.html)) | TV pool not covering the president |

On April 15, 2025, the White House said outlets would be eligible for the pool "regardless of the substantive viewpoint expressed by an outlet"; the AP called the removal of the wire seat "a grave disservice to the American people" ([Fox News](https://www.foxnews.com/media/associated-press-reuters-rip-trump-white-house-cutting-wire-service-slot-press-pool)).

## What happened to the TV pool in September 2026?

On September 18, 2026, President Donald Trump announced that CNN, MS NOW and Politico would be banned from the White House, describing their coverage as "FICTION and LIES" ([NPR](https://www.npr.org/2026/09/19/nx-s1-5974854/trump-cnn-msnow-politico-ban); [record](/incidents/2026-white-house-bans-cnn-msnow-politico)). On September 19, their reporters were denied entry at the gates after their hard passes, the standing credentials that let reporters enter the White House press area, were deactivated ([record](/incidents/2026-white-house-bans-cnn-msnow-politico)).

After the White House deactivated the passes, banning CNN from its scheduled pool duty on Monday, September 21, the other pool reporters' networks said, "There will be no replacement pool put in place" ([AP via Action News Now](https://www.actionnewsnow.com/news/major-tv-networks-stand-with-cnn-decline-to-replace-its-white-house-pool-crew/article_47bdc4b7-11bd-5c5a-a581-dabefc858a0b.html)). The pool's email to subscribers said, "Effective today, there would be no network pool coverage of the president's events" ([AP via MPR News](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/09/22/what-is-the-white-house-pool-its-a-battleground-between-trump-and-free-press-rights)). RSF reported that Bryan Boughton, Fox News' Washington bureau chief, coordinates the television pool ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/usa-white-house-media-ban-robs-public-access-independent-presidential-coverage)).

The three news outlets sued on September 21, 2026, in Cable News Network, Inc. v. Trump, No. 1:26-cv-03287, which is pending with a hearing scheduled for September 23 ([case record](/cases/cnn-msnow-politico-v-trump-2026)).

## Do other governments control press access the same way?

The record files these actions under [access bans](/tactics/access_ban), and the [access-ban ladder](/ladders/access_ban) sets them beside other countries' cases. In the Philippines on February 21, 2018, a Rappler reporter was told she was barred from Malacañang Palace, the seat of the presidency, on President Rodrigo Duterte's orders; his spokesperson cited "fake news" ([record](/incidents/2018-philippines-bans-rappler-presidential-palace)). In Hungary on March 10, 2026, a mayor from the governing Fidesz party removed two Telex reporters from a campaign forum ([record](/incidents/2026-hungary-mayor-removes-telex-reporters)).

title: What is a White House hard pass?
dek: A hard pass is the standing credential that lets a reporter enter the White House without applying each day. Who issues it, how, and when it was revoked.
body_md:
A White House hard pass is the standing credential, issued by the White House Press Office, that lets a journalist who covers the president of the United States enter the White House grounds and press areas without applying for entry each day ([glossary: hard pass](/glossary/hard-pass)). White House staff can suspend or revoke hard passes, and United States courts have required notice, a chance to respond and written reasons before a pass is denied ([Sherrill v. Knight](/cases/sherrill-v-knight-1977)).

## What is a hard pass, and what does it allow?

The White House is the office and residence of the president of the United States in Washington, D.C., and the White House press corps is the group of journalists who report from it. "Reporters who regularly cover the White House are issued 'hard passes' to enter the complex," according to the White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA), the organization of reporters who cover the president ([WHCA](https://whca.press/covering-the-white-house/); [glossary: WHCA](/glossary/whca)). The WHCA wrote that the passes "allow access to the White House campus, without having to apply for a temporary pass each day" ([WHCA](https://whca.press/covering-the-white-house/)).

A hard pass is not needed to attend press briefings. The WHCA says that "any journalist can attend the briefings, even if their outlet doesn't have an assigned seat," and that "others can get a temporary pass through the White House Press Office" ([WHCA](https://whca.press/covering-the-white-house/)). That temporary credential is a [day pass](/glossary/day-pass), which requires a new application for each day. The WHCA describes the hard pass as "an important convenience for those who regularly cover the White House" because it lets journalists enter "without permission ahead of time" ([WHCA](https://whca.press/covering-the-white-house/)).

The hard pass is separate from two other arrangements that shape White House coverage. Seats in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room are assigned by the WHCA board, which has done so "since the Reagan administration," under President Ronald Reagan; there are 49 seats, with the Associated Press in the front row centre ([WHCA](https://whca.press/covering-the-white-house/)). The [press pool](/glossary/press-pool), the small rotating group of reporters who cover the president in spaces too small for the whole press corps, was chosen by the WHCA until February 25, 2025, when the White House took over the selection ([record](/incidents/2025-whca-loses-control-of-press-pool)). On the White House grounds the pool is "typically a group of 20 correspondents from wire services, print outlets, TV and radio, along with photojournalists and sound operators," and the WHCA wrote that "AP, Bloomberg and Reuters have permanent slots in the pool" ([WHCA](https://whca.press/covering-the-white-house/)). Those permanent slots for wire services ended on April 15, 2025, when the White House announced that the three agencies would compete for a single rotating seat ([record](/incidents/2025-white-house-cuts-wire-service-pool-slot)).

The process by which a government body decides which journalists receive such credentials is called [credentialing](/glossary/credentialing). The record files government decisions about individual reporters' passes and accreditation under [credential control](/tactics/credential_control), and decisions to bar reporters from rooms, buildings and trips under [access bans](/tactics/access_ban).

## Can anybody get a press pass to the White House?

A journalist who covers the White House regularly can apply. "To get a hard pass, journalists must submit an application to the White House Press Office and undergo a background screening by the Secret Service, which protects the President and is responsible for security at the White House," the WHCA wrote, adding that "this process can take several months" ([WHCA](https://whca.press/covering-the-white-house/); [glossary: Secret Service](/glossary/secret-service)). The WHCA itself "doesn't issue credentials or control who can enter the White House complex or briefing room" ([WHCA](https://whca.press/covering-the-white-house/)).

The process was described in detail in a 1977 court opinion. In the 1970s, the Press Office first checked that the applicant held a pass for the House and Senate press galleries of the United States Congress, lived in the Washington area and needed to report from the White House regularly, which was usually confirmed by an editor; the application then went to the Secret Service "for a security check, including a background FBI investigation" ([Sherrill v. Knight opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)). "Whether a pass is then issued depends solely on the recommendation of the Secret Service," the court wrote. The opinion records that "as of March 5, 1975, there were apparently 1,589 outstanding White House press passes" ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)).

In 2019, during the first presidency of Donald Trump, the White House applied a new standard. According to the Columbia Journalism Review (CJR), a magazine about journalism, on May 9, 2019, journalists had to be present in the White House "for at least 90 days out of a 180-day period" to qualify for a hard pass, and "virtually the entire press corps failed to meet this new test, including all six of the Post's White House correspondents," citing Washington Post columnist Dana Milbank ([CJR](https://www.cjr.org/the_media_today/white-house-press-passes.php)). Outlets applied for exceptions for senior journalists or accepted six-month passes, and the press secretary told the Post the change was a result of security concerns, CJR reported ([CJR](https://www.cjr.org/the_media_today/white-house-press-passes.php)).

## Can the White House take away a journalist's hard pass?

It can, but the D.C. Circuit, the federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., has set limits. In Sherrill v. Knight, decided on December 15, 1977, the court held that the First Amendment, the part of the United States Constitution that protects freedom of the press, "requires that this access not be denied arbitrarily or for less than compelling reasons" ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json); [case record](/cases/sherrill-v-knight-1977)). It required "notice of the factual bases for denial, an opportunity for the applicant to respond to these, and a final written statement of the reasons for denial" ([case record](/cases/sherrill-v-knight-1977)). The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press (RCFP), a United States non-profit that gives legal help to journalists, filed a brief in the case with the WHCA and the National Press Club; it argued that "a system of licensing access to news which is not bounded by constitutional safeguards is open to the abuse of excluding those whose sole crime is opposition to the government" ([RCFP](https://www.rcfp.org/karem-dc-circuit-press-pass-ruling/)). That case concerned a pass that was never issued; the court wrote in a footnote that it had "no occasion" to consider revocation of "an already-issued White House press pass" ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)).

On November 7, 2018, after a news conference with President Donald Trump, the White House suspended the hard pass of CNN correspondent Jim Acosta ([record](/incidents/2018-white-house-revokes-acosta-press-pass)). Press Secretary Sarah Sanders said the White House would never tolerate "a reporter placing his hands on a young woman just trying to do her job as a White House intern," a description CNN disputed ([Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2018/11/8/white-house-suspends-cnns-acosta-after-trump-confrontation)). On November 16, 2018, a federal judge, Timothy J. Kelly, granted CNN a temporary restraining order on due process grounds drawn from Sherrill ([case record](/cases/cnn-v-trump-2018)). On November 19, the White House told Acosta "your hard pass is restored," and CNN dropped the suit ([Yahoo News / AP](https://news.yahoo.com/white-house-restores-jim-acosta-212020316.html)). The WHCA later wrote that when "the Trump White House attempted to revoke a journalist's hard pass," it "advocated directly with the Administration and in federal court" ([WHCA](https://whca.press/covering-the-white-house/)).

On August 16, 2019, the White House press secretary suspended the credentials of Brian Karem, White House correspondent for Playboy, for 30 days after an exchange with a former presidential adviser in the Rose Garden ([RCFP](https://www.rcfp.org/briefs-comments/karem-v-trump/)). The lower court, the federal trial court in Washington, ruled in Karem's favour in September 2019, and the Department of Justice appealed; the RCFP and a coalition of 44 media organizations supported Karem on appeal ([RCFP](https://www.rcfp.org/karem-dc-circuit-press-pass-ruling/)). In June 2020, a D.C. Circuit panel held that the suspension likely violated his Fifth Amendment right to due process; Judge David S. Tatel wrote that "the White House may not rely on unarticulated standards of professionalism" and that "forty years on, today's hard-pass system is little changed from the one described in Sherrill" ([Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press](https://www.rcfp.org/karem-dc-circuit-press-pass-ruling/)). The court also wrote that the White House could still order "the immediate removal of rogue, mooning journalists" to keep order at events ([RCFP](https://www.rcfp.org/karem-dc-circuit-press-pass-ruling/)). Sam Donaldson, a former ABC News journalist who held White House credentials for more than 50 years, said no administration before Trump's had revoked a reporter's White House press pass over coverage or behaviour while reporting, according to the RCFP ([RCFP](https://www.rcfp.org/karem-dc-circuit-press-pass-ruling/)).

## What happened to hard passes in 2025 and 2026?

In February 2025, the White House began excluding the Associated Press from the Oval Office and Air Force One, and on February 25, 2025, it took over selection of the press pool from the WHCA ([record](/incidents/2025-white-house-bars-ap-gulf-of-america); [record](/incidents/2025-whca-loses-control-of-press-pool)). On October 31, 2025, it announced that reporters would need an appointment to enter "Upper Press," the West Wing offices of the press secretary and senior press aides; a White House memo said the policy "will ensure adherence to best practices pertaining to access to sensitive material" ([U.S. Press Freedom Tracker](https://pressfreedomtracker.us/all-incidents/white-house-restricts-reporter-access-to-press-secretary-staffs-offices/); [record](/incidents/2025-white-house-restricts-access-to-upper-press-office)).

A separate credential system applies at the Pentagon, the headquarters of the Department of Defense, the United States military department. On September 19, 2025, the department issued rules that required reporters to pledge not to solicit or publish unauthorized information; most credentialed news organizations declined to sign and turned in their badges from October 15, 2025 ([record](/incidents/2025-pentagon-issues-new-press-credentialing-rules); [record](/incidents/2025-pentagon-press-corps-forfeits-badges)). Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said, "Wear a badge and follow the rules," and added, "or go home" ([Wikipedia summary of reporting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Pentagon_press_pass_forfeiture)).

On September 18, 2026, Trump announced on Truth Social, a social media platform, that CNN, MS NOW and Politico would be banned from the White House, and described their coverage as "FICTION and LIES" ([NPR](https://www.npr.org/2026/09/19/nx-s1-5974854/trump-cnn-msnow-politico-ban)). On September 19, the Secret Service turned away CNN's Betsy Klein, MS NOW's Akayla Gardner and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett at the gates after their hard passes were deactivated ([record](/incidents/2026-white-house-bans-cnn-msnow-politico)). One of the reporters said she was told "they had to take my badge because it was disabled" ([ABC News](https://abcnews.com/Politics/trump-banning-cnn-msnow-politico-white-house/story?id=136569980)). The White House has not said which story or stories prompted the decision (as of 2026-09-22).

Banning CNN also affected pool duty. CNN had been scheduled as the television pool network on September 21, 2026, and the other networks declined to replace it; Reporters Without Borders (RSF), a press freedom organization based in Paris, reported that the television pool would not cover presidential events "going forward" ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/usa-white-house-media-ban-robs-public-access-independent-presidential-coverage)). The outlets sued on September 21, 2026, in Cable News Network, Inc. v. Trump, No. 1:26-cv-03287, which is pending before a federal judge, with a hearing scheduled for September 23, 2026 ([case record](/cases/cnn-msnow-politico-v-trump-2026)). The outlets say the deactivation of their hard passes violated their First Amendment rights and their Fifth Amendment right to due process ([AP via MPR News](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/09/22/what-is-the-white-house-pool-its-a-battleground-between-trump-and-free-press-rights)).

### Hard-pass and pool changes, 1966 to 2026

| Date | Action | Outcome, as of 2026-09-22 |
|---|---|---|
| 1966-05-03 | Secret Service denies Robert Sherrill a pass | Court requires notice and written reasons, 1977 ([case](/cases/sherrill-v-knight-1977)) |
| 2018-11-07 | Acosta hard pass suspended | Restored 2018-11-19 ([record](/incidents/2018-white-house-revokes-acosta-press-pass)) |
| 2019 | 90-of-180-days standard for hard passes | Exceptions and six-month passes issued ([CJR](https://www.cjr.org/the_media_today/white-house-press-passes.php)) |
| 2019-08-16 | Karem credentials suspended for 30 days | Suspension blocked on appeal, 2020 ([RCFP](https://www.rcfp.org/karem-dc-circuit-press-pass-ruling/)) |
| 2025-02-25 | White House takes over pool selection | In effect ([record](/incidents/2025-whca-loses-control-of-press-pool)) |
| 2025-10-31 | Upper Press closed without appointment | In effect ([record](/incidents/2025-white-house-restricts-access-to-upper-press-office)) |
| 2026-09-19 | CNN, MS NOW, Politico hard passes deactivated | Case pending ([record](/incidents/2026-white-house-bans-cnn-msnow-politico)) |

## Is the swimming pool still under the White House press room?

The briefing room sits over the old indoor pool. According to the White House Historical Association, the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room was built in 1969 and 1970, authorized by President Richard M. Nixon, as "a one-story Briefing Room installed over the swimming pool built for President Franklin Delano Roosevelt in 1933" ([White House Historical Association](https://www.whitehousehistory.org/the-president-the-press-and-proximity)). Pool reporters have travelled with presidents since Roosevelt's time, and three wire reporters were with him at Warm Springs, Georgia, when he died in 1945 ([WHCA](https://whca.press/covering-the-white-house/)).

## How do other countries issue passes to reporters who cover the government?

Other governments also issue credentials that decide who may enter official buildings, and the record sets them side by side on the [access-ban ladder](/ladders/access_ban). In Türkiye, the Council of State, the country's top administrative court, suspended 2018 rules under which the presidency's Communications Directorate could deny or cancel the press cards that let reporters enter official buildings ([record](/incidents/2021-turkiye-press-card-controls-restrictive)). In Kazakhstan, rules adopted in August 2024 allow a journalist's accreditation to be withdrawn for six months over conduct at a news event, including off-topic questions ([record](/incidents/2024-kazakhstan-restrictive-media-accreditation-rules)). In Belarus, on August 29, 2020, the government withdrew the accreditation of at least 17 journalists working for foreign outlets ([record](/incidents/2020-belarus-strips-accreditation-foreign-outlets)).

title: The Espionage Act and journalists: prosecutions, leak cases and the press
dek: How the United States Espionage Act of 1917 has been used against the press and journalists' sources, from The Masses to Julian Assange, with outcomes.
body_md:
The Espionage Act is a United States law, first passed in 1917, that makes it a crime to obtain, keep or pass on information relating to national defence without authorization, and it has been used mostly against government employees and contractors who gave classified information to journalists ([glossary: Espionage Act](/glossary/espionage-act)). The one publisher indicted under it in the record is Julian Assange of WikiLeaks, charged in 2019 over the publication of classified military and diplomatic documents, who pleaded guilty to a single count in June 2024 ([record](/incidents/2019-us-assange-espionage-act-indictment)).

## What is the Espionage Act?

Congress, the national legislature of the United States, passed the Espionage Act in June 1917, during World War I, making it a crime to interfere with military recruitment or operations ([record](/incidents/1917-us-espionage-act-bars-the-masses-from-the-mail); [glossary: Congress](/glossary/us-congress)). Its main provisions are now in chapter 37 of title 18 of the United States Code, the collection of federal criminal laws ([glossary](/glossary/espionage-act)). Prosecutions under this and similar laws in other countries are grouped under the tactic [secrets and espionage laws](/tactics/secrets_and_espionage_laws), defined as laws that make it a crime to obtain, keep or disclose information a government has classified.

### What does the law say?

Section 793 of title 18 covers anyone who, having "unauthorized possession of, access to, or control over" any document "relating to the national defense, or information relating to the national defense which information the possessor has reason to believe could be used to the injury of the United States or to the advantage of any foreign nation, willfully communicates, delivers, transmits" it "to any person not entitled to receive it" ([18 U.S.C. § 793(e), Cornell Law School](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/793)). A parallel clause, section 793(d), applies to people who hold the material lawfully, such as officials with security clearances. A person convicted "shall be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than ten years, or both" ([18 U.S.C. § 793](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/793)).

The statute does not mention journalists or news organizations. It applies to "whoever" communicates national defense information to a person not entitled to receive it, and to anyone who conspires to do so ([18 U.S.C. § 793(g)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/793)). Whether that language reaches a reporter who receives classified information from a source and publishes it is the question behind most debate about Espionage Act journalists.

### Who uses the Espionage Act, and against whom?

The Department of Justice, the United States federal department that prosecutes federal crimes, brings Espionage Act prosecutions ([glossary](/glossary/us-department-of-justice)). The act "has increasingly been used against government employees and contractors who leak classified information to journalists, rather than against spies working for other governments," according to the [glossary entry](/glossary/espionage-act). A [leak investigation](/glossary/leak-investigation) is the government inquiry into who disclosed the information, and it can include collecting journalists' phone and email records.

## How was the Espionage Act used against the press in World War I?

The first uses of the Espionage Act against publications came through the post office, not the courts. In 1917, New York's postmaster, Thomas Patten, declared the August 1917 issue of The Masses, an anti-war socialist magazine, unmailable under the act because of cartoons and articles opposing the war and the draft ([record](/incidents/1917-us-espionage-act-bars-the-masses-from-the-mail)). Patten found the material likely, in the language of the Espionage Act, to cause insubordination in the armed forces and to obstruct recruiting.

Judge Learned Hand of the federal district court in New York, a trial court, ruled for the magazine. He wrote: "If one stops short of urging upon others that it is their duty or their interest to resist the law, it seems to me one should not be held to have attempted to cause its violation" ([MTSU](https://firstamendment.mtsu.edu/article/masses-publishing-co-v-patten-s-d-n-y/)). The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed Hand later in 1917, the mail ban stood, and The Masses stopped publishing within months ([record](/incidents/1917-us-espionage-act-bars-the-masses-from-the-mail)).

The Post Office, led by Postmaster General Albert Burleson, also revoked the second-class mailing rate of the Milwaukee Leader, a socialist daily, over articles opposing the war ([record](/incidents/1917-us-burleson-mail-ban-milwaukee-leader)). On March 7, 1921, the Supreme Court of the United States, the country's highest court, upheld the revocation 7 to 2. The majority wrote that "the Constitution was adopted to preserve our Government, not to serve as a protecting screen for those who while claiming its privileges seek to destroy it" ([MTSU](https://firstamendment.mtsu.edu/article/united-states-ex-rel-milwaukee-social-democratic-publishing-co-v-burleson/)). Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes dissented: "The use of the mails is almost as much a part of free speech as the right to use our tongues."

"By 1918, in actions that seriously threatened First Amendment freedoms and that likely would not be upheld today, 74 newspapers had been denied mailing privileges," according to the First Amendment Encyclopedia of Middle Tennessee State University ([MTSU](https://firstamendment.mtsu.edu/article/espionage-act-of-1917/)).

### The Second World War

In the Second World War the United States relied on a voluntary code rather than prosecutions. On December 19, 1941, twelve days after Japan's bombing of the United States naval base at Pearl Harbor, President Franklin Roosevelt created the Office of Censorship under Byron Price, a former executive news editor of the Associated Press, which wrote a Code of Wartime Practices for newspapers and radio stations. The code asked editors not to publish "troop, ship, and plane movements, fortifications, weather conditions, casualty lists, damage to various military targets," among other military secrets, and publishers followed it without a formal enforcement mechanism, according to EBSCO Research Starters. Roosevelt said: "All Americans abhor censorship, just as they abhor war." The office was abolished after Japan's surrender in 1945.

## Has any reporter been charged under the Espionage Act?

As of September 22, 2026, the record holds one indictment under the act of a person who published classified information, and one case in which a reporter was named as a possible co-conspirator but not charged.

### Julian Assange (2019 to 2024)

On May 23, 2019, the Justice Department added 17 counts under the Espionage Act to an existing charge against Julian Assange, founder of WikiLeaks, a website that publishes leaked documents ([record](/incidents/2019-us-assange-espionage-act-indictment)). The counts concerned WikiLeaks' 2010 publication of classified military reports and diplomatic cables supplied by Chelsea Manning, a United States Army intelligence analyst.

Assistant Attorney General John Demers said, "Julian Assange is no journalist, this is made plain by the totality of his conduct as alleged in the indictment," and the department said Assange's actions "risked serious harm to United States national security to the benefit of our adversaries" ([ABC News](https://abcnews.com/Politics/julian-assange-charged-18-count-indictment-wikileaks-disclosures/story?id=63234593)). His lawyer, Barry Pollack, said: "These unprecedented charges demonstrate the gravity of the threat the criminal prosecution of Julian Assange poses to all journalists" ([ABC News](https://abcnews.com/Politics/julian-assange-charged-18-count-indictment-wikileaks-disclosures/story?id=63234593)).

Assange was then in British custody. After five years in a British prison contesting extradition, he pleaded guilty in June 2024 to "a single criminal count of conspiring to obtain and disclose classified US national defense documents," was sentenced to time served and was released ([Gulf News](https://gulfnews.com/amp/world/americas/wikileaks-julian-assange-to-be-freed-after-pleading-guilty-to-us-espionage-charge-1.1719284494426); [record](/incidents/2019-us-assange-espionage-act-indictment)). The plea ended the prosecution without a court ruling on whether publishing classified documents is protected by the First Amendment, the part of the United States Constitution that protects freedom of the press ([glossary](/glossary/first-amendment)).

### James Rosen (2013)

In 2009, Fox News reporter James Rosen published a story, based on a State Department analyst's account, that North Korea would likely respond to United Nations sanctions with more nuclear tests ([record](/incidents/2013-us-doj-names-fox-reporter-co-conspirator)). An FBI agent's 2010 warrant affidavit, reported in May 2013, said Rosen, "in his newsgathering, was violating federal statutes that prohibit 'unauthorized disclosure of national defense information' as an 'aider, abettor, and/or co-conspirator'" ([Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press](https://www.rcfp.org/justice-search-warrant-relied-probable-cause-criminal-conduct-fox-ne/)). The warrant was used to obtain two days of Rosen's personal emails, his phone records and records of his security-badge movements inside the State Department. The analyst, Stephen Kim, pleaded guilty. Rosen was never charged ([record](/incidents/2013-us-doj-names-fox-reporter-co-conspirator)).

The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), a non-profit organization in New York, said that "U.S. government efforts to prosecute leakers by obtaining information from journalists has a chilling effect domestically and sends a terrible message to journalists around the world" ([CPJ, 2013-05-20](https://cpj.org/2013/05/cpj-alarmed-by-us-justice-scrutiny-of-fox-news-rep/)).

## How has the act been used against journalists' sources?

Most Espionage Act prosecutions connected to the press have charged the person who gave information to a reporter. In October 2013, CPJ reported that "six government employees, plus two contractors including Edward Snowden, have been subjects of felony criminal prosecutions since 2009 under the 1917 Espionage Act, accused of leaking classified information to the press" ([CPJ, 2013-10-10](https://cpj.org/reports/2013/10/obama-and-the-press-us-leaks-surveillance-post-911/)). Across all earlier United States administrations there had been three such prosecutions, according to CPJ ([record](/incidents/2013-obama-doj-charges-eight-under-espionage-act)).

### Leak cases under the Obama administration (2009 to 2013)

The Project On Government Oversight, a United States watchdog group, wrote that the Justice Department under President Barack Obama and Attorney General Eric Holder "has used it more than all prior administrations combined" ([POGO](https://www.pogo.org/analyses/six-americans-obama-and-holder-charged-under-espionage-act-and-one-bonus-whistleblower)). Matthew Miller, then spokesman for Attorney General Eric Holder, told CPJ: "It was never a conscious decision to bring more of these cases than we ever had. It was a combination of things" ([CPJ](https://cpj.org/reports/2013/10/obama-and-the-press-us-leaks-surveillance-post-911/)). One source told the report's author, "I worry now about calling somebody because the contact can be found out through a check of phone records or e-mails" ([CPJ](https://cpj.org/reports/2013/10/obama-and-the-press-us-leaks-surveillance-post-911/)). The Freedom of the Press Foundation, a United States non-profit that builds secure communication tools for newsrooms, later said the pattern set a precedent that later administrations, including Donald Trump's first, could extend ([record](/incidents/2013-obama-doj-charges-eight-under-espionage-act); [glossary](/glossary/freedom-of-the-press-foundation)).

### The Pentagon Papers (1971)

The Pentagon Papers case shows the government using a different tool against the press itself: prior restraint, an order to stop publication before it happens ([glossary: prior restraint](/glossary/prior-restraint)). Daniel Ellsberg, a military analyst, copied a classified Department of Defense history of United States involvement in Vietnam and gave it to The New York Times, which began publishing excerpts on June 13, 1971 ([record](/incidents/1971-us-pentagon-papers-injunction)). On June 15, 1971, the Department of Justice obtained a temporary restraining order from a federal court against the New York Times, and later sought one against The Washington Post.

On June 30, 1971, in New York Times Co. v. United States, the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that the government had not met its burden. The Court wrote that "any system of prior restraints of expression comes to this Court bearing a heavy presumption against its constitutional validity," and Justice Hugo Black wrote that "the press was protected so that it could bare the secrets of government and inform the people" ([Justia](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/403/713/)). Both the New York Times and the Washington Post resumed publishing. Government lawyers had argued that publication would cause grave and irreparable harm to national security ([record](/incidents/1971-us-pentagon-papers-injunction)).

### Chelsea Manning (2010 to 2017)

In 2010, Chelsea Manning gave WikiLeaks a large archive of military reports and diplomatic cables, which WikiLeaks and news partners including The Guardian and The New York Times published in part ([record](/incidents/2010-us-chelsea-manning-espionage-act-wikileaks)). The Army charged her under the Espionage Act and with "aiding the enemy." In 2013 a military court convicted her on Espionage Act counts, acquitted her of aiding the enemy and sentenced her to 35 years, which the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) called "the heaviest sentence handed down to a whistleblower or leaker in U.S. history" ([ACLU](https://www.aclu.org/news/free-speech/chelsea-manning-case-timeline)). President Obama commuted the sentence in January 2017 ([record](/incidents/2010-us-chelsea-manning-espionage-act-wikileaks)). Military prosecutors said her disclosures endangered lives and national security. The ACLU said: "When a soldier who shared information with the press and public is punished far more harshly than others who tortured prisoners and killed civilians, something is seriously wrong with our justice system" ([ACLU](https://www.aclu.org/news/free-speech/chelsea-manning-case-timeline)).

### John Kiriakou (2012 to 2013)

John Kiriakou, a former officer of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), the United States foreign intelligence agency, pleaded guilty in October 2012 to one count under the Espionage Act for identifying a covert CIA officer to a freelance journalist, who did not publish the name ([record](/incidents/2012-us-john-kiriakou-espionage-act-cia-torture-source)). United States Attorney Neil MacBride said, "John Kiriakou put the life of a covert officer at risk; he put the officer's family in danger; and he exposed our nation's vital secrets" ([ABC News](https://abcnews.com/Blotter/john-kiriakou-30-months/story?id=18314999)). On January 25, 2013, Judge Leonie Brinkema sentenced him to 30 months.

### James Risen and the Sterling case (2008 to 2015)

James Risen, a New York Times reporter, wrote in a 2006 book about a CIA operation aimed at Iran's nuclear program ([record](/incidents/2014-us-james-risen-subpoena-jeffrey-sterling)). Prosecutors identified Jeffrey Sterling, a former CIA officer, as a suspect and, from 2008, sought to make Risen testify before a grand jury and at trial. In 2013 the Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit ruled that reporters had no First Amendment privilege to withhold a source's identity in a criminal case, and the Supreme Court declined to hear Risen's appeal in 2014. Attorney General Eric Holder then approved "a limited subpoena to compel Risen to testify, but it does not permit prosecutors to ask Risen the identity of his source" ([CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/official-prosecutors-will-subpoena-reporter-james-risen)). In October 2014 the department said it would not force Risen to testify, and the former CIA officer was convicted in January 2015 without Risen's testimony ([record](/incidents/2014-us-james-risen-subpoena-jeffrey-sterling)).

## Can the government jail reporters who refuse to name a source?

It has done so in a leak case outside the Espionage Act. In Branzburg v. Hayes, on June 29, 1972, the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4 that reporters have the same obligation as other citizens to answer relevant questions before a grand jury, a panel that decides whether to bring criminal charges ([record](/incidents/1972-us-branzburg-v-hayes-reporters-privilege)). A [subpoena](/glossary/subpoena) is the legal order that compels such testimony.

On July 6, 2005, a federal judge, Thomas F. Hogan, jailed Judith Miller of The New York Times for contempt after she refused to name a source to a grand jury investigating the disclosure of the identity of Valerie Plame, a CIA officer ([record](/incidents/2005-us-judith-miller-jailed-plame-source)). Miller said: "If journalists cannot be trusted to keep confidences, then journalists cannot function and there cannot be a free press" ([RCFP](https://www.rcfp.org/reporter-judith-miller-jailed-refusing-reveal-plame-case-source/)). She was released on September 29, 2005, after 85 days, when her source released her from confidentiality. Cases like Miller's and Risen's are why journalists say they must protect sources even at the cost of a contempt finding, since a reporter who cannot keep a promise of confidentiality may not get the information at all.

The United States has no federal [shield law](/glossary/shield-law), a statute letting journalists refuse to disclose sources; federal cases are governed by Justice Department guidelines instead ([glossary](/glossary/shield-law)). That gap is separate from the Whistleblower Protection Act, a federal law that shields many government workers who report government wrongdoing through official channels but does not extend the same protection to intelligence-agency employees who instead give classified information to a reporter. Reporters Without Borders (RSF), a press freedom organization based in Paris, wrote that "the PRESS Act, a federal shield law, failed to pass for a second successive time in 2024" ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/country/united-states)).

### Leak investigations and reporters' records, 2013 to 2025

In May 2013, the Associated Press (AP) disclosed that the Justice Department had obtained telephone records for more than 20 of its phone lines while investigating who had disclosed a classified CIA operation in Yemen ([record](/incidents/2013-us-doj-seizes-ap-phone-records)). AP President Gary Pruitt said, "There can be no possible justification for such an over-broad collection of the telephone communications of The Associated Press and its reporters" ([Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2013/5/14/us-government-seized-ap-phone-records)). The department said it followed "all applicable laws, federal regulations, and Department of Justice policies." More than 100 journalists worked in the offices whose numbers were collected ([Lawfare](https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/ap-doj-secretly-obtained-ap-reporters-phone-call-records)). The department issued revised media-subpoena guidelines on July 12, 2013 ([record](/incidents/2013-us-doj-seizes-ap-phone-records)).

In 2021, the Justice Department notified The New York Times, The Washington Post and CNN that it had secretly obtained reporters' phone records, and in the Times' case sought email records, in leak investigations that began under the first Trump administration; in one case a nondisclosure order barred Times executives from disclosing the request ([record](/incidents/2021-doj-bans-seizing-reporters-records-garland)). President Joe Biden said: "Absolutely, positively it's wrong. It's simply, simply wrong" ([Axios](https://www.axios.com/doj-leaks-journalist-records-6bfa8da3-d20a-4b29-b50b-c6d6780556f0)).

On July 19, 2021, Attorney General Merrick Garland barred the department from using subpoenas, warrants or court orders to obtain journalists' records in leak investigations, with narrow exceptions ([record](/incidents/2021-doj-bans-seizing-reporters-records-garland)). The memo said that "a free and independent press is vital to the functioning of our democracy" ([CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/merrick-garland-justice-department-subpoenas-reporters/)).

On April 25, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi rescinded those rules ([record](/incidents/2025-doj-rescinds-media-subpoena-guidelines)). Her memo said: "Federal government employees intentionally leaking sensitive information to the media undermines the ability of the Department of Justice to uphold the rule of law, protect civil rights, and keep America safe" ([RCFP](https://www.rcfp.org/doj-rescinds-news-media-guidelines-analysis/)). The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, a United States non-profit that gives legal help to journalists, said that "by their nature, leak investigations chill newsgathering and reporting in the public interest." As of September 22, 2026, the sources cited do not report whether the department has subpoenaed a journalist under the restored rules.

## Is the United States arresting journalists?

The record holds arrests and detentions of journalists in the United States, none of them under the Espionage Act. On May 29, 2020, Minnesota State Patrol troopers arrested a CNN crew, correspondent Omar Jimenez, photojournalist Leonel Mendez and producer Bill Kirkos, during a live broadcast in Minneapolis; they were released about ninety minutes later and Governor Tim Walz apologized the same day ([record](/incidents/2020-minnesota-state-patrol-arrests-cnn-crew-minneapolis)). RSF reported that Mario Guevara, a Spanish-language reporter originally from El Salvador, was arrested while livestreaming a protest in the state of Georgia on June 14, 2025, and deported on October 3, 2025 ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/usa-8-ways-trump-shrinking-space-press-freedom-literally)). RSF's barometer listed one journalist detained in the United States as of September 22, 2026 ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/country/united-states)).

In the second Trump administration, under President Trump, the Department of Defense cited leaks when it issued press credential rules on September 19, 2025, calling them "an important step in preventing leaks that damage operational security and national security" ([record](/incidents/2025-pentagon-issues-new-press-credentialing-rules)). Some press freedom lawyers describe rules of that kind as a speech restriction on newsgathering rather than a narrow security measure. The rules required reporters to pledge not to solicit or publish unauthorized information; a federal judge ruled against parts of them in March and April 2026, and the department appealed.

## How do other countries use secrets and espionage laws against journalists?

The record's [ladder for secrets and espionage laws](/ladders/secrets_and_espionage_laws) sets the United States cases beside those of other countries. Each country's law is its own.

In Myanmar, on September 3, 2018, a court sentenced Reuters reporters Wa Lone and Kyaw Soe Oo to seven years under the Official Secrets Act, a law from the period of British rule, after police handed them documents at a dinner shortly before arresting them; they had been investigating the killing of ten Rohingya men and boys ([record](/incidents/2018-myanmar-reuters-journalists-official-secrets-act)). President Win Myint pardoned them on May 7, 2019, after 511 days in prison.

In Russia, on September 5, 2022, a Moscow court sentenced Ivan Safronov, a former military correspondent for Kommersant and Vedomosti, to 22 years for treason, accusing him of spying for a foreign country ([record](/incidents/2022-russia-safronov-treason-sentence)). On July 19, 2024, a Russian judge sentenced Wall Street Journal correspondent Evan Gershkovich to 16 years on an espionage charge; he was released on August 1, 2024, in a prisoner exchange ([record](/incidents/2024-russia-sentences-gershkovich)).

In China, a court sentenced Dong Yuyu, an editor at the state newspaper Guangming Daily, to seven years for espionage in November 2024, after his arrest at lunch with a Japanese diplomat in February 2022 ([record](/incidents/2024-china-dong-yuyu-espionage-sentence)).

In the United Kingdom, on August 18, 2013, officers detained David Miranda, partner of Guardian journalist Glenn Greenwald, for nine hours at Heathrow Airport under Schedule 7 of the Terrorism Act 2000; the government said he was suspected of carrying "highly sensitive stolen information that would help terrorism" ([record](/incidents/2013-uk-miranda-detention-guardian-hard-drives)). In Australia, on June 5, 2019, federal police searched the headquarters of the Australian Broadcasting Corporation over its "Afghan Files" reports on alleged killings by special forces, under a warrant citing the Crimes Act 1914's ban on "publishing classified material"; prosecutors decided in October 2020 not to charge the journalist ([record](/incidents/2019-australia-afp-raids-abc-afghan-files)).

In Zimbabwe, President Emmerson Mnangagwa signed the Patriotic Act on July 14, 2023, which makes it a crime to meet foreign governments with intent to damage the country's sovereignty ([record](/incidents/2023-zimbabwe-patriotic-act-criminalizes-foreign-contact)). Information Minister Monica Mutsvangwa said it did not criminalize journalists' ordinary work.

## Espionage Act and the press: a timeline, 1917 to 2025

| Date | Case | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| 1917-06 | Congress passes the Espionage Act | In force, amended ([Cornell](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/793)) |
| 1917 | The Masses barred from the mail | Ban upheld on appeal, 1917 ([record](/incidents/1917-us-espionage-act-bars-the-masses-from-the-mail)) |
| 1921-03-07 | Milwaukee Leader mailing rate case | Supreme Court upheld 7 to 2 ([record](/incidents/1917-us-burleson-mail-ban-milwaukee-leader)) |
| 1971-06-30 | Pentagon Papers injunction | Lifted, 6 to 3 ([record](/incidents/1971-us-pentagon-papers-injunction)) |
| 2010 | Chelsea Manning charged | Convicted 2013; commuted 2017 ([record](/incidents/2010-us-chelsea-manning-espionage-act-wikileaks)) |
| 2013-01-25 | John Kiriakou sentenced | 30 months ([record](/incidents/2012-us-john-kiriakou-espionage-act-cia-torture-source)) |
| 2013-05-20 | James Rosen named in warrant | Not charged ([record](/incidents/2013-us-doj-names-fox-reporter-co-conspirator)) |
| 2013-10-10 | CPJ counts eight leak prosecutions since 2009 | Report ([record](/incidents/2013-obama-doj-charges-eight-under-espionage-act)) |
| 2015-01 | Sterling convicted without Risen's testimony | Convicted ([record](/incidents/2014-us-james-risen-subpoena-jeffrey-sterling)) |
| 2019-05-23 | Julian Assange indicted on 17 counts | Guilty plea to one count, 2024 ([record](/incidents/2019-us-assange-espionage-act-indictment)) |
| 2025-04-25 | Justice Department restores subpoena balancing test | In effect ([record](/incidents/2025-doj-rescinds-media-subpoena-guidelines)) |

## Is publishing classified information different from leaking it?

The Espionage Act does not distinguish between a source and a publisher, but prosecutors have. In the cases in the record from 2009 to 2015, the people charged were government officials or contractors, several of them in the intelligence community, who had lawful access to classified information and passed it on, under section 793(d) or similar provisions; the reporters who received it, including Risen and Rosen, were subpoenaed or searched but not charged ([record](/incidents/2013-obama-doj-charges-eight-under-espionage-act); [record](/incidents/2013-us-doj-names-fox-reporter-co-conspirator)). Press freedom groups have said that using the act to prosecute journalists themselves, rather than only the government officials and federal workers who give them information, would be a significant expansion of how it has been applied since 1917. The Assange indictment in 2019 charged the receipt and publication of classified documents, which Assange's lawyer said is conduct news organizations routinely engage in ([record](/incidents/2019-us-assange-espionage-act-indictment)).

The Justice Department's position in 2019 was that Assange was not a journalist. Demers said the totality of his alleged conduct made that "plain" ([ABC News](https://abcnews.com/Politics/julian-assange-charged-18-count-indictment-wikileaks-disclosures/story?id=63234593)). Press freedom organizations, including CPJ, have described leak prosecutions and the collection of reporters' records as a deterrent to sources who would otherwise speak about national security ([CPJ](https://cpj.org/reports/2013/10/obama-and-the-press-us-leaks-surveillance-post-911/)).

## What protects journalists who publish classified information?

In the United States, the protections come from court rulings and department policy rather than from the Espionage Act itself. The Pentagon Papers ruling of 1971 sets a "heavy presumption" against orders stopping publication ([Justia](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/403/713/)). No court has ruled on whether First Amendment protections bar an Espionage Act prosecution of a journalist who publishes classified information, because the Assange prosecution ended in a plea (as of 2026-09-22); the record includes no successful prosecution of a traditional news reporter, as distinct from a source, for publishing rather than leaking classified material.

Protection from subpoenas and searches depends on Justice Department rules. After the Rosen warrant and the seizure of AP phone records became public, guidelines issued by Attorney General Eric Holder in July 2013 restricted subpoenas naming reporters as suspects ([record](/incidents/2013-us-doj-names-fox-reporter-co-conspirator)). The 2021 Garland rules went further and barred compulsory process against journalists in leak investigations; the 2025 Bondi memo returned the department to a balancing test that weighs law enforcement interests against press freedom ([record](/incidents/2025-doj-rescinds-media-subpoena-guidelines)). Each change applied to all federal leak cases, whatever the administration.

For sources, the protection is narrower. The officials and contractors charged from 2009 to 2013 were accused of leaking classified information to the press, and the statute's penalty of up to ten years applies to them whether or not a story was published ([CPJ](https://cpj.org/reports/2013/10/obama-and-the-press-us-leaks-surveillance-post-911/); [18 U.S.C. § 793](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/793)). In the Kiriakou case, the journalist did not publish the covert officer's name, and Kiriakou was still sentenced to 30 months ([record](/incidents/2012-us-john-kiriakou-espionage-act-cia-torture-source)).

title: What is "government censorship" of journalists? Methods, examples and outcomes
dek: The methods governments use to restrict journalists, from prior restraint and licensing to shutdowns and prosecutions, with dated examples by country.
body_md:
Governments restrict journalists in several documented ways: they review or block articles before publication, license and close outlets, withdraw credentials and access, prosecute reporters and their sources, watch their communications, cut their funding, expel foreign correspondents, shut down the internet, and detain or harm reporters ([tactics](/tactics)). Press freedom organizations such as the Committee to Protect Journalists call many of these actions "censorship," while the governments involved usually cite national security, public order or false information as the reason ([CPJ](https://cpj.org/about/faq/)). This page is for readers, researchers and journalists who need the specific method behind the broad label "government censorship," because the record shows a courtroom or a policy response differs by tactic, not just by the fact that a government restricted the press.

## What is "government censorship" of journalists?

The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), a non-profit organization in New York that documents cases of journalists imprisoned or killed, uses the category "Censored" for journalists or outlets "officially suppressed or banned; editions confiscated; news outlets closed" ([CPJ FAQ](https://cpj.org/about/faq/)). CPJ counts separate categories, among them "Imprisoned," "Expelled," "Threatened" and "Harassed," and "Legal Action," which it defines as "credentials denied or suspended; fined; sentenced to prison; visas denied or canceled; restrictive legislation; libel suit intended to inhibit coverage" ([CPJ FAQ](https://cpj.org/about/faq/)).

Reporters Without Borders (RSF), a press freedom organization based in Paris, measures instead whether journalists "are free to work without censorship or judicial sanctions" as one part of its legal indicator ([RSF methodology](https://rsf.org/en/methodology-used-compiling-world-press-freedom-index-2026)). RSF's mandate is "in the spirit of Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights," the 1948 United Nations declaration of human rights ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/who-are-we)).
