The record uses thirteen named tactics rather than a single word, so that each action can be described by what was done ([tactics](/tactics)). The sections below follow that list, with dated examples from many countries and the outcome of each.

## Can a government stop the press from publishing?

Some governments can, under their own laws, and some courts have limited the power. In the United States, the Supreme Court held in 1931, in Near v. Minnesota, that a state law used to shut a Minneapolis weekly was a restraint on publication in advance that the Constitution did not allow ([record](/incidents/1931-us-near-v-minnesota-gag-law)). In 1971, in the Pentagon Papers case, it wrote that "any system of prior restraints of expression comes to this Court bearing a heavy presumption against its constitutional validity" ([Justia](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/403/713/)).

Other countries have used advance review as ordinary law. In Israel, the government kept a British-era Press Ordinance in 1948 that gave a military press reviewer power to block publication on security grounds. In India, on June 26, 1975, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's government required every newspaper to obtain government clearance before publishing, during a national state of emergency that lasted until March 21, 1977.

## What are some examples of government restrictions on journalists?

### Prior restraint: review before publication

[Prior restraint](/glossary/prior-restraint) is an order or rule that stops something from being published before it appears ([tactic](/tactics/prior_restraint)). In Soviet Russia, the government led by Vladimir Lenin created Glavlit in 1922, a central office that reviewed manuscripts, newspapers and plays before release; by 1930 all printing needed its approval. In the United States, on December 19, 1941, President Franklin Roosevelt created the Office of Censorship, whose press code was voluntary. In Türkiye, the broadcasting regulator RTÜK fined three television channels in February 2023 after they aired criticism of the government's earthquake response ([record](/incidents/2023-turkiye-rtuk-fines-earthquake-coverage)).

### Licensing and closure of outlets

Governments that license newspapers or broadcasters can refuse, suspend or cancel the licence ([tactic](/tactics/outlet_licensing)). In Venezuela, the government let Radio Caracas Television's broadcast concession expire on May 27, 2007, and described the non-renewal as "natural and inexorable" ([record](/incidents/2007-venezuela-rctv-license-not-renewed)). In Hungary, the Media Council ended Klubradio's terrestrial licence in February 2021, saying its application was "incorrect, incomplete and contradictory" ([record](/incidents/2021-hungary-klubradio-loses-broadcast-license)). In Myanmar, the military revoked five media outlets' licences on March 8, 2021, weeks after seizing power ([record](/incidents/2021-myanmar-junta-revokes-media-licenses)). In China's Hong Kong, Apple Daily printed its final edition in June 2021 after the authorities froze its parent company's assets under the National Security Law ([record](/incidents/2021-hong-kong-apple-daily-forced-closure)).

### Credential control: who counts as a journalist

Credential control means deciding who may work as a reporter through passes, accreditation or licences ([tactic](/tactics/credential_control)). Germany's Editors Law of October 4, 1933, under Chancellor Adolf Hitler's government, required journalists to register with a state press chamber and barred Jewish journalists from the profession ([record](/incidents/1933-germany-editors-law)). Zimbabwe's Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act of 2002 required every journalist and media company to hold a government licence ([record](/incidents/2002-zimbabwe-aippa-media-licensing)). In the United States, the Department of Defense issued press credential rules on September 19, 2025, which most news organizations refused to sign; the Defense Department said the rules were "an important step in preventing leaks" ([record](/incidents/2025-pentagon-issues-new-press-credentialing-rules)).

### Access bans: keeping reporters out of places

An access ban bars reporters from briefings, buildings, pools or trips ([tactic](/tactics/access_ban)). On September 18, 2026, Donald Trump, the president of the United States, announced that CNN, MS NOW and Politico would be banned from the White House, his office and residence, describing their coverage as "FICTION and LIES" ([NPR](https://www.npr.org/2026/09/19/nx-s1-5974854/trump-cnn-msnow-politico-ban); [record](/incidents/2026-white-house-bans-cnn-msnow-politico)). RSF described restrictions on journalists' physical presence at White House press conferences and other events, the State Department and the Pentagon, writing that one way "to alienate the press is by limiting their physical presence in key government spaces" ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/usa-8-ways-trump-shrinking-space-press-freedom-literally)). Since October 2023, Israel has barred foreign journalists covering the Gaza Strip from entering it independently, telling its Supreme Court in January 2026 that the ban should stay for "security reasons" ([record](/incidents/2026-israel-maintains-ban-on-foreign-press-access-to-gaza)).

### Secrets and espionage laws

These laws make it a crime to obtain or disclose information a government has classified ([tactic](/tactics/secrets_and_espionage_laws)). In Myanmar, a court sentenced Reuters reporters Wa Lone and Kyaw Soe Oo to seven years under the Official Secrets Act on September 3, 2018; they were pardoned on May 7, 2019 ([record](/incidents/2018-myanmar-reuters-journalists-official-secrets-act)). In the United States, the Espionage Act of 1917 has been used mainly against officials who gave information to journalists, and in 2019 against Julian Assange of WikiLeaks ([record](/incidents/2019-us-assange-espionage-act-indictment)).

### Insult, defamation and "false information" laws

These laws make it a crime to insult a head of state, damage a reputation or publish what the government declares false ([tactic](/tactics/insult_and_defamation_laws)). In Thailand, a court sentenced magazine editor Somyot Prueksakasemsuk to 11 years on January 24, 2013, under Article 112 of the penal code, which bars insults to the royal family ([record](/incidents/2013-thailand-somyot-lese-majeste-sentence)). On March 4, 2022, Russia's parliament made it a crime, punishable by up to 15 years, to publish information about the military that contradicts official statements; the speaker, Vyacheslav Volodin, said it was needed "to protect our soldiers and officers, and to protect the truth" ([record](/incidents/2022-russia-criminalizes-fake-war-reports)). In India, on February 10, 2026, a court sentenced the journalist Ravi Nair to one year in prison for criminal defamation ([record](/incidents/2026-india-journalist-sentenced-adani-defamation)).

### Surveillance, subpoenas and spyware

Governments collect journalists' records and communications, often to find their sources ([tactic](/tactics/surveillance_and_subpoenas)). In Mexico, research groups documented Pegasus spyware sent to the journalist Carmen Aristegui in 2017; the government denied sending it ([record](/incidents/2017-mexico-aristegui-pegasus-spyware)). In Hungary, Amnesty International found traces of Pegasus on the phone of the investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi in 2021 ([record](/incidents/2021-hungary-panyi-pegasus-spyware)). In the United States, the Department of Justice obtained two months of Associated Press phone records in a leak investigation, disclosed in May 2013 ([record](/incidents/2013-us-doj-seizes-ap-phone-records)).

### Funding and ownership pressure

Governments can act through money or through owners instead of against reporters, withholding financial support or redirecting it to favored outlets ([tactic](/tactics/funding_and_ownership_pressure)). Egypt's government placed every newspaper and magazine under state ownership by decree on May 24, 1960 ([record](/incidents/1960-egypt-nasser-nationalizes-press)). In Hungary, owners aligned with the governing party donated 476 outlets to one foundation, KESMA, in November 2018, and the government exempted the merger from antitrust review ([record](/incidents/2018-hungary-kesma-media-merger)). In Argentina, President Javier Milei's government shut the state news agency Télam in March 2024 ([record](/incidents/2024-argentina-milei-closes-telam)). In the United States, on May 1, 2025, the president signed Executive Order 14290 directing an end to federal funding for NPR and PBS, which said public funding for news was "corrosive to the appearance of journalistic independence" ([record](/incidents/2025-trump-order-ends-cpb-funding-npr-pbs)).

### Expulsion of foreign journalists and visa denial

Governments can expel foreign journalists or refuse them visas ([tactic](/tactics/expulsion_and_visa_denial)). On February 19, 2020, China's foreign ministry expelled three Wall Street Journal correspondents over an opinion headline that a ministry spokesperson called "racist" ([record](/incidents/2020-china-expels-three-wsj-journalists-headline)). In May 2022, Russia closed the Moscow bureau of CBC/Radio-Canada, the Canadian public broadcaster, and cancelled its journalists' visas ([record](/incidents/2022-russia-expels-cbc-cancels-visas)). In Ethiopia, the media regulator gave The Economist's correspondent Tom Gardner 48 hours to leave on May 13, 2022 ([record](/incidents/2022-ethiopia-expels-tom-gardner)). In the United States, the Department of Homeland Security proposed a rule in August 2025 under which visas used by foreign journalists "would be restricted to 90 days for Chinese nationals and 240 days for citizens of other countries," according to RSF ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/usa-8-ways-trump-shrinking-space-press-freedom-literally)).

### Internet shutdowns and blocking

A shutdown cuts internet or phone service so that audiences cannot receive news and reporters cannot send it ([tactic](/tactics/shutdowns_and_blocking)). India cut internet and phone service across Jammu and Kashmir from August 5, 2019, citing public order and security ([record](/incidents/2019-india-kashmir-communications-blackout)). Iran reduced internet connectivity to about five percent of normal for nearly a week during protests in November 2019 ([record](/incidents/2019-iran-nationwide-internet-shutdown)). In India in August 2023, the news outlet Gaon Savera's Facebook page and X account (formerly Twitter) were blocked without a public explanation ([record](/incidents/2023-india-blocks-gaon-savera-accounts)). Russia's media regulator blocked the news sites of BBC Russian, Deutsche Welle and Meduza in March 2022, cutting off internet users inside Russia from independent reporting on the war ([record](/incidents/2022-russia-blocks-bbc-dw-meduza)).

### Detention, prosecution and violence

The record includes harm to journalists where a government actor was involved ([tactic](/tactics/detention_and_violence)). On October 2, 2018, Saudi agents killed the journalist Jamal Khashoggi inside Saudi Arabia's consulate in Istanbul ([record](/incidents/2018-saudi-arabia-khashoggi-killed-consulate)). In Egypt, security forces arrested Al Jazeera English journalists Peter Greste, Mohamed Fahmy and Baher Mohamed on December 29, 2013; they were later convicted and then pardoned ([record](/incidents/2013-egypt-al-jazeera-journalists-jailed)). In China's Hong Kong, the High Court sentenced the media owner Jimmy Lai to 20 years on February 8, 2026 ([record](/incidents/2025-hong-kong-convicts-jimmy-lai-under-national-security-law)). CPJ counted 336 journalists imprisoned as of December 1, 2025 ([CPJ](https://cpj.org/about/)).

### Lawsuits by officials

Officials sometimes sue journalists and outlets ([tactic](/tactics/lawsuits_against_press)). In Malta, the economy minister had the journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia's bank account frozen in February 2017, months before she was killed ([record](/incidents/2017-malta-freezes-caruana-galizia-account)). In the Philippines, a Manila court convicted Maria Ressa of Rappler of cyber libel on June 15, 2020 ([record](/incidents/2020-philippines-ressa-cyber-libel-conviction)). In the United States, President Trump sued The New York Times for $15 billion in September 2025 ([record](/incidents/2025-trump-sues-new-york-times-15-billion)).

### Official labels: "foreign agent" and "fake news"

Some governments officially label outlets as foreign agents or sources of false news ([tactic](/tactics/disinformation_labeling); [glossary: foreign agent law](/glossary/foreign-agent-law)). On April 23, 2021, Russia's Justice Ministry labelled the independent site Meduza a "foreign agent" ([record](/incidents/2021-russia-designates-meduza-foreign-agent)). In Georgia, parliament passed a law in May 2024 requiring media that receive 20 percent or more of their funding from abroad to register ([record](/incidents/2024-georgia-foreign-influence-law)). In India, the Bombay High Court struck down a government "fact check unit" rule in September 2024, finding its key terms "vague and overbroad" ([record](/incidents/2024-india-court-strikes-down-fact-check-unit)).

## How have these methods changed since 1900?

The record is organized by decade as well as by tactic, and the methods in use have shifted over time ([era: 1910s](/eras/1910s)). This history runs from mail bans and formal state press offices to the licensing, labelling and shutdown tools used today.

### 1900 to 1945: mail bans and state press offices

In the First World War, the United States Post Office used the Espionage Act to bar anti-war publications such as The Masses from the mail in 1917 ([record](/incidents/1917-us-espionage-act-bars-the-masses-from-the-mail)). In the 1930s, Portugal's government under António de Oliveira Salazar formally established press controls under a new constitution in 1933, and Brazil's government under Getúlio Vargas created a state department with broad press powers in 1939 ([record](/incidents/1939-brazil-vargas-creates-dip)). Spain's Press Law of April 1938, under Francisco Franco, required government permission to found a newspaper or work as a journalist ([record](/incidents/1938-spain-franco-press-law)).

### 1946 to 1999: coups, martial law and emergencies

After seizing or suspending power, several governments closed the press all at once. In the Philippines, President Ferdinand Marcos closed every major news outlet under martial law on September 21, 1972 ([record](/incidents/1972-philippines-marcos-martial-law-media-closures)). In Chile, the armed forces shut down opposition radio stations and newspapers on the day of the September 11, 1973 coup ([record](/incidents/1973-chile-coup-press-shutdown)). In Poland, General Wojciech Jaruzelski's martial law of December 13, 1981, suspended nearly all newspapers ([record](/incidents/1981-poland-martial-law-press-suspended)).

### 2000 to 2026: licences, labels, spyware and shutdowns

Entries from 2000 onward include administrative and technical tools: media licensing laws such as Zimbabwe's in 2002, "foreign agent" labels in Russia and Georgia, spyware found on journalists' phones in Mexico, Morocco and Hungary, and internet shutdowns in India, Iran, Ethiopia and Tanzania ([record](/incidents/2002-zimbabwe-aippa-media-licensing); [record](/incidents/2021-russia-designates-meduza-foreign-agent); [record](/incidents/2020-morocco-omar-radi-pegasus-and-detention); [record](/incidents/2025-tanzania-internet-shutdown-election-day)). Tanzania cut national internet traffic by nearly 90 percent on October 29, 2025, election day ([record](/incidents/2025-tanzania-internet-shutdown-election-day)).

## How do these restrictions affect the public?

Press freedom organizations describe the effect on audiences, not only on reporters. RSF wrote on September 22, 2026, that the White House ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico "is really a ban on the public's access to the American presidency," in the words of Clayton Weimers, executive director of RSF North America ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/usa-white-house-media-ban-robs-public-access-independent-presidential-coverage)). RSF wrote in its review of access restrictions in the United States that they mean "journalists are unable to ask important questions, break important stories and keep the public informed," and called on the administration to rescind them "to ensure government transparency and accountability" ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/usa-8-ways-trump-shrinking-space-press-freedom-literally)).

The United Nations reports that "self-censorship has grown by more than 60%, driven by fear of reprisals, online harassment, judicial intimidation, and economic pressure," citing UNESCO's World Trends Report 2022 to 2025 ([United Nations](https://www.un.org/en/observances/press-freedom-day)); when reporters hold back stories they would otherwise publish, public opinion forms on a narrower range of reporting than existed before.

## What reasons do governments give?

The stated justification is recorded in each government's own words, and the reason a political leader gives in public is not always the reason a court later accepts. Israel's government cited "security reasons" for the Gaza ban ([record](/incidents/2026-israel-maintains-ban-on-foreign-press-access-to-gaza)). The Royal Canadian Mounted Police, Canada's federal police, said restrictions on reporters at the Fairy Creek logging blockades in British Columbia were "reasonably necessary" because of terrain, space and poor phone coverage ([record](/incidents/2021-rcmp-restricts-press-fairy-creek-court-order)). The United Kingdom said in 2013 that David Miranda was suspected of carrying "highly sensitive stolen information that would help terrorism" ([record](/incidents/2013-uk-miranda-detention-guardian-hard-drives)). The Philippine president's spokesperson said in 2018 that President Rodrigo Duterte had "lost trust" in Rappler's "fake news" reporting ([record](/incidents/2018-philippines-bans-rappler-presidential-palace)).

## What happens when courts review these actions?

Outcomes differ by country and court. In Canada, a British Columbia judge found on July 20, 2021, that the police had not justified their exclusion zones, and ordered them to keep in mind the media's role in a free and democratic society ([record](/incidents/2021-rcmp-restricts-press-fairy-creek-court-order)). In Australia, the High Court ruled on April 15, 2020, that the warrant used to search the journalist Annika Smethurst's home was invalid ([record](/incidents/2020-australia-high-court-invalidates-smethurst-warrant)). In the United Kingdom, the Court of Appeal ruled in January 2016 that Miranda's detention was lawful but that the stop power was incompatible with protections for journalistic material ([record](/incidents/2013-uk-miranda-detention-guardian-hard-drives)). In the United States, a federal judge ruled against the Pentagon's credential rules in March 2026, and the Defense Department appealed ([record](/incidents/2025-pentagon-issues-new-press-credentialing-rules)).

### Selected examples and outcomes

| Date | Country | Action | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1922 | Russia (USSR) | Glavlit created | Dissolved 1991 |
| 1975-06-26 | India | Pre-publication clearance for all newspapers | Lifted 1977-03-21 |
| 2007-05-27 | Venezuela | RCTV concession not renewed ([record](/incidents/2007-venezuela-rctv-license-not-renewed)) | Sustained |
| 2018-09-03 | Myanmar | Reuters reporters sentenced ([record](/incidents/2018-myanmar-reuters-journalists-official-secrets-act)) | Pardoned 2019-05-07 |
| 2019-08-05 | India | Kashmir communications cut ([record](/incidents/2019-india-kashmir-communications-blackout)) | Ongoing |
| 2021-07-20 | Canada | Court limits RCMP exclusion zones ([record](/incidents/2021-rcmp-restricts-press-fairy-creek-court-order)) | Reversed by court |
| 2022-03-04 | Russia | Law on "false" military reports ([record](/incidents/2022-russia-criminalizes-fake-war-reports)) | In force |
| 2024-09 | India | Fact check unit rule struck down ([record](/incidents/2024-india-court-strikes-down-fact-check-unit)) | Reversed by court |
| 2025-09-19 | United States | Pentagon credential rules ([record](/incidents/2025-pentagon-issues-new-press-credentialing-rules)) | On appeal |
| 2026-09-19 | United States | White House hard passes deactivated ([record](/incidents/2026-white-house-bans-cnn-msnow-politico)) | Case pending |

## Which laws protect journalists in different countries?

Each country's protection is set by its own constitution, statutes and courts, and one country's law is not a measure for another's. In the United States, the [First Amendment](/glossary/first-amendment) to the Constitution provides that Congress shall make no law "abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press" ([glossary](/glossary/first-amendment)); free speech and press freedom overlap in this and other legal systems, though a constitution can protect one without fully protecting the other. In Canada, section 2(b) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms protects "freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, including freedom of the press and other media of communication" ([Government of Canada](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/const/page-12.html)). In the United Kingdom, Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights, given effect by the Human Rights Act 1998, provides that "everyone has the right to freedom of expression," and also that it "shall not prevent States from requiring the licensing of broadcasting, television or cinema enterprises" ([Human Rights Act 1998, Schedule 1](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1998/42/schedule/1)). At the international level, Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted by the United Nations in 1948, is the reference RSF cites for its own mandate ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/who-are-we)); that declaration lists freedom of expression among the fundamental rights it sets out for every country.

Written guarantees do not settle every case. The Supreme Court of the United States ruled 5 to 4 in 1972 that reporters have no constitutional privilege to refuse to answer a grand jury's questions ([record](/incidents/1972-us-branzburg-v-hayes-reporters-privilege)), and India required pre-publication clearance of every newspaper under a declared state of emergency from 1975 to 1977.

## Where does the USA rank in press freedom?

In RSF's 2026 World Press Freedom Index, the United States ranks 64th of 180 countries and territories, down from 57th in 2025 ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/country/united-states)). The [United States overview](/united-states) lists the dated actions behind the country's entries.

## What are the consequences of a censure?

A censure is a different thing from the restrictions above. It is a formal statement of disapproval, for example by a legislature against one of its own members; it does not stop anyone from publishing. The restrictions described in this article are actions by governments that limit what journalists can gather, publish or distribute.

## Why does press freedom matter for democracy?

The United Nations writes that "press freedom and independent journalism are key to peace, economic recovery, sustainable development, and human rights" ([United Nations](https://www.un.org/en/observances/press-freedom-day)). It notes that information manipulation, "including the use of AI by malicious actors," is weakening trust, and that World Press Freedom Day, May 3, was proclaimed by the General Assembly in December 1993. CPJ states on its website that "without a free press, few other human rights are attainable" ([CPJ FAQ](https://cpj.org/about/faq/)). In the United States, a 2021 Department of Justice memo said that "a free and independent press is vital to the functioning of our democracy" ([record](/incidents/2021-doj-bans-seizing-reporters-records-garland)).

## Who documents restrictions on journalists?

Press freedom organizations and news media document cases and publish their methods. CPJ says it works in "more than 120 countries" and that each case it classifies "is corroborated by more than one source for factual accuracy" ([CPJ FAQ](https://cpj.org/about/faq/)). RSF publishes the annual World Press Freedom Index ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/who-are-we)). In the United States, the U.S. Press Freedom Tracker, run by the Freedom of the Press Foundation, records incidents ([glossary](/glossary/us-press-freedom-tracker)).

title: Is it legal to ban reporters from the White House?
dek: What United States courts have held about barring reporters from the White House, from Sherrill v. Knight (1977) to the 2026 CNN, MS NOW and Politico case.
body_md:
United States courts have held that the White House may not deny a reporter's press pass "arbitrarily or for less than compelling reasons" and must give notice, a chance to respond and written reasons ([Sherrill v. Knight, 1977](/cases/sherrill-v-knight-1977)), but in 2025 an appeals court allowed the White House to exclude the AP news agency from the Oval Office and the president's aircraft, which it treated as restricted spaces ([AP v. Budowich](/cases/ap-v-budowich-2025)). The lawsuit over President Donald Trump's ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico is pending as of September 22, 2026 ([case record](/cases/cnn-msnow-politico-v-trump-2026)).

## Is it legal to ban reporters from the White House?

The White House is the office and residence of the president of the United States in Washington, D.C. Two constitutional rights apply. The [First Amendment](/glossary/first-amendment) provides that Congress shall make no law "abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press." The Fifth Amendment guarantees [due process](/glossary/due-process), fair procedure before the government takes away a person's liberty or property ([glossary](/glossary/fifth-amendment)). Because losing a hard pass affects a reporter's ability to do their job, courts have treated it as a protected liberty interest, which is why Sherrill v. Knight required notice and a chance to respond before one is denied.

In 1977 the D.C. Circuit, the federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., held that once press facilities are open to journalists, the First Amendment "requires that this access not be denied arbitrarily or for less than compelling reasons" ([opinion, 569 F.2d 124](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)). The court also wrote that "arbitrary or content-based criteria for press pass issuance are prohibited under the first amendment" ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)).

Under the [public forum doctrine](/glossary/public-forum-doctrine), United States courts give the government broad discretion over access to spaces such as the Oval Office, the president's office. Treating speakers differently because of their opinions is [viewpoint discrimination](/glossary/viewpoint-discrimination), which courts disfavour. Courts have described a free press as playing an essential role in a democracy, and freedom of the press is widely treated as a fundamental right under the First Amendment, even though the case law above shows that right is not absolute inside the White House.

## What have courts decided in earlier White House cases?

### Sherrill v. Knight (1977)

Robert Sherrill of The Nation was denied a White House press pass in 1966 on the recommendation of the Secret Service, the federal agency that protects the president ([opinion](https://static.case.law/f2d/569/cases/0124-01.json)). The court held that a denial requires "notice of the factual bases for denial, an opportunity for the applicant to respond to these, and a final written statement of the reasons for denial" ([case record](/cases/sherrill-v-knight-1977)).

### CNN and Jim Acosta (2018)

On November 7, 2018, the White House suspended CNN correspondent Jim Acosta's hard pass, the credential that let him enter the White House grounds without applying each day, after a news conference with President Donald Trump ([record](/incidents/2018-white-house-revokes-acosta-press-pass)). On November 16, 2018, Judge Timothy J. Kelly of the federal trial court in Washington granted a temporary restraining order on due process grounds, and the White House restored the pass on November 19 ([case record](/cases/cnn-v-trump-2018)).

### Brian Karem (2019 to 2020)

On August 16, 2019, Press Secretary Stephanie Grisham suspended Playboy correspondent Brian Karem's credentials for 30 days after an exchange in the Rose Garden ([RCFP](https://www.rcfp.org/karem-dc-circuit-press-pass-ruling/)). In June 2020 a D.C. Circuit panel held that "the White House may not rely on unarticulated standards of professionalism" to justify the suspension, Judge David S. Tatel wrote ([RCFP, 2020-06-11](https://www.rcfp.org/karem-dc-circuit-press-pass-ruling/)).

### The Associated Press (2025)

From February 11, 2025, the Trump administration excluded Associated Press (AP) journalists from the Oval Office and Air Force One, the president's aircraft, after the AP kept the name "Gulf of Mexico" ([record](/incidents/2025-white-house-bars-ap-gulf-of-america)). On April 8, 2025, Judge Trevor N. McFadden ordered access restored; on June 6, 2025, a D.C. Circuit panel stayed that order 2 to 1 except for the East Room ([case record](/cases/ap-v-budowich-2025)). Judge Neomi Rao wrote that "these restricted presidential spaces are not First Amendment fora opened for private speech and discussion" ([CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2025/06/06/politics/white-house-ban-associated-press-continue)). The Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University tracks the [case](https://knightcolumbia.org/cases/the-associated-press-v-budowich).

## Which media are banned from the White House?

As of September 22, 2026, three restrictions on news outlets are in effect. Reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico (the three outlets banned on September 18, 2026) cannot enter the White House grounds with their hard passes, which were deactivated on September 19, 2026 ([record](/incidents/2026-white-house-bans-cnn-msnow-politico)). The AP remains excluded from the Oval Office, the presidential aircraft, Mar-a-Lago and the Cabinet Room ([record](/incidents/2025-white-house-bars-ap-gulf-of-america)). Reporters Without Borders (RSF), a press freedom organization based in Paris, reported that Trump banned The Wall Street Journal's reporters from the presidential plane on trips in 2025 after a story about Trump and Jeffrey Epstein ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/usa-8-ways-trump-shrinking-space-press-freedom-literally)). Losing a rotation slot cuts off an outlet's White House coverage for as long as the exclusion lasts, since a barred reporter cannot file from inside the building at all.

## What journalists are banned from the White House?

On September 19, 2026, the Secret Service turned away CNN's Betsy Klein, MS NOW's Akayla Gardner and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett, who were denied entry at the gates ([record](/incidents/2026-white-house-bans-cnn-msnow-politico)). One said she was told "they had to take my badge because it was disabled" ([ABC News](https://abcnews.com/Politics/trump-banning-cnn-msnow-politico-white-house/story?id=136569980)). On September 21, CNN was kept from its scheduled turn in the White House press pool ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/usa-white-house-media-ban-robs-public-access-independent-presidential-coverage)).

## What reason did President Trump give for the ban?

On September 18, 2026, President Donald Trump announced the ban on Truth Social, a social media platform, and described the outlets' coverage as "FICTION and LIES" ([NPR](https://www.npr.org/2026/09/19/nx-s1-5974854/trump-cnn-msnow-politico-ban)). The same day he told a Bloomberg reporter, "I dislike dishonest press, like you. I think you're terrible" ([NPR](https://www.npr.org/2026/09/19/nx-s1-5974854/trump-cnn-msnow-politico-ban)). The AP reported that he cited "fake news" ([AP via MPR News](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/09/22/what-is-the-white-house-pool-its-a-battleground-between-trump-and-free-press-rights)). The White House has not named a specific story (as of 2026-09-22).

## What do the three news organizations and press groups say?

The three news outlets sued the Trump administration on September 21, 2026, after MS NOW journalists were denied access to the White House ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/white-house/ms-now-journalists-denied-access-white-house-trump-announced-ban-rcna598677)). The complaint says: "This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles" ([PBS NewsHour](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/cnn-ms-now-politico-say-theyve-notified-trump-theyre-suing-over-denied-white-house-access)). The outlets said in a statement that they were suing "to protect our First Amendment rights" ([Axios](https://www.axios.com/2026/09/21/trump-cnn-msnow-politico-suit)), and their public statements indicate they intend to vigorously defend that claim in court.

The White House Correspondents' Association, the organization of reporters who cover the president, said on September 18, 2026: "The Constitution protects the freedom of the press from government interference" ([WHCA](https://whca.press/2026/09/18/statement-on-white-house-position-on-cnn-msnow-and-politico/)). A CNN spokesperson said that if the ban went ahead, "it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right," according to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), a non-profit in New York ([CPJ](https://cpj.org/2026/09/cpj-president-trumps-arbitrary-cnn-ms-now-politico-ban-violates-first-amendment-rights/)). CPJ said the ban "violates First Amendment rights" ([CPJ](https://cpj.org/2026/09/cpj-president-trumps-arbitrary-cnn-ms-now-politico-ban-violates-first-amendment-rights/)).

On September 21, 2026, other news organizations, including the AP, The New York Times and The Washington Post, joined a CPJ statement saying the ban "sets a dangerous precedent, one in which the President decides what the American people can know and from whom they can know it" ([CPJ](https://cpj.org/2026/09/leading-news-outlets-issue-statement-in-defense-of-a-us-free-press/)). The signatories stand "in our firm defense of a free press" ([CPJ](https://cpj.org/2026/09/leading-news-outlets-issue-statement-in-defense-of-a-us-free-press/)). Press freedom groups frame the dispute as being about the American people's press access to the presidency and the independent journalism that access makes possible; other outlets were not named in the September 2026 ban, but CPJ's "dangerous precedent" language reflects concern that they could face similar action.

## Is criticizing the president of the United States a crime?

The First Amendment bars laws "abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press" ([glossary](/glossary/first-amendment)), but in 1798 President John Adams signed the Sedition Act, which made it a crime to "print, utter, or publish ... any false, scandalous, and malicious writing" about the government, according to the National Archives as cited by the [AP](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/09/22/what-is-the-white-house-pool-its-a-battleground-between-trump-and-free-press-rights).

## What happens next in the 2026 case?

Cable News Network, Inc. v. Trump, No. 1:26-cv-03287, was filed on September 21, 2026, in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia ([case record](/cases/cnn-msnow-politico-v-trump-2026)). It is assigned to Judge Timothy Kelly, and a hearing is scheduled for September 23, 2026 ([PBS NewsHour](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/cnn-ms-now-politico-say-theyve-notified-trump-theyre-suing-over-denied-white-house-access); [record](/incidents/2026-white-house-bans-cnn-msnow-politico)).

### White House access cases, 1966 to 2026

| Date | Action | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| 1966-05-03 | Secret Service denies Robert Sherrill a press pass | Procedures required, 1977-12-15 ([case](/cases/sherrill-v-knight-1977)) |
| 2018-11-07 | Acosta hard pass suspended | Restored 2018-11-19 ([case](/cases/cnn-v-trump-2018)) |
| 2019-08-16 | Karem pass suspended 30 days | Suspension blocked, 2020 ([RCFP](https://www.rcfp.org/karem-dc-circuit-press-pass-ruling/)) |
| 2025-02-11 | AP excluded from Oval Office and presidential plane | Partly in effect; on appeal ([case](/cases/ap-v-budowich-2025)) |
| 2026-09-19 | CNN, MS NOW, Politico press passes deactivated | Pending ([case](/cases/cnn-msnow-politico-v-trump-2026)) |

## Have other governments barred reporters from the seat of government?

The record files these cases under [access bans](/tactics/access_ban) and compares them on the [access-ban ladder](/ladders/access_ban). In the Philippines, on February 21, 2018, a Rappler reporter was barred from Malacañang Palace on President Rodrigo Duterte's orders, and his spokesperson cited the outlet's "fake news" reporting ([record](/incidents/2018-philippines-bans-rappler-presidential-palace)). In Kazakhstan, 2024 rules let officials withdraw accreditation for off-topic questions ([record](/incidents/2024-kazakhstan-restrictive-media-accreditation-rules)).

title: Where does the United States rank on the World Press Freedom Index?
dek: In RSF's 2026 World Press Freedom Index the United States ranks 64th of 180. Its rank by year since 2013, how the index works, and who ranks first.
body_md:
In the 2026 World Press Freedom Index published by Reporters Without Borders (RSF), the United States ranks 64th of 180 countries and territories, with a score of 62.61 out of 100 ([RSF, United States](https://rsf.org/en/country/united-states)). That is seven places lower than its 2025 rank of 57th, and RSF writes that the country "is experiencing a significant and prolonged decline in press freedom" ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/country/united-states)). This page tracks the press freedom index United States score has received every year since 2013, and how the ranking is calculated.

## Where does the United States rank on the World Press Freedom Index in 2026?

The United States is 64th of 180 in the 2026 index, with a global score of 62.61 ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/country/united-states)). In 2025 it was 57th, with a score of 65.487. RSF's 2026 global analysis lists as one of five findings: "The United States has fallen seven places and other countries in the Americas, such as Ecuador and Peru, have plummeted in the ranking" ([RSF, 2026 analysis](https://rsf.org/en/2026-rsf-index-press-freedom-25-year-low)).

RSF places every country in one of five categories by score. A score from 55 to 70 is "problematic," the category the United States is in for 2026 ([RSF methodology](https://rsf.org/en/methodology-used-compiling-world-press-freedom-index-2026)). The [United States overview](/united-states) and the [country profile](/countries/us) show the RSF rank beside dated incidents.

### United States scores on the five indicators, 2026

RSF gives each country a rank and a score from 0 to 100 on five indicators ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/country/united-states)):

| Indicator | 2026 rank | 2026 score |
|---|---|---|
| Political context | 62 | 53.59 |
| Economic context | 41 | 55.05 |
| Legal framework | 52 | 70.47 |
| Sociocultural context | 66 | 64.27 |
| Safety | 98 | 69.68 |

In 2025 the United States ranked 41st on the political indicator and 91st on safety, according to RSF ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/country/united-states)).

## How has the United States ranked by year?

RSF's yearly index tables give the following ranks and scores for the United States. RSF describes its current method as applying "from 2022 onwards," so scores before and after 2022 were calculated in different ways ([RSF methodology](https://rsf.org/en/methodology-used-compiling-world-press-freedom-index-2026)). Canada, the northern neighbour of the United States, is shown for comparison.

| Year | United States rank | United States score | Canada rank | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2013 | 32 | 81.78 | 20 | [RSF 2013](https://rsf.org/en/index?year=2013) |
| 2014 | 46 | 76.51 | 18 | [RSF 2014](https://rsf.org/en/index?year=2014) |
| 2015 | 49 | 75.59 | 8 | [RSF 2015](https://rsf.org/en/index?year=2015) |
| 2016 | 41 | 77.51 | 18 | [RSF 2016](https://rsf.org/en/index?year=2016) |
| 2017 | 43 | 76.12 | 22 | [RSF 2017](https://rsf.org/en/index?year=2017) |
| 2018 | 45 | 76.27 | 18 | [RSF 2018](https://rsf.org/en/index?year=2018) |
| 2019 | 48 | 74.31 | 18 | [RSF 2019](https://rsf.org/en/index?year=2019) |
| 2020 | 45 | 76.15 | 16 | [RSF 2020](https://rsf.org/en/index?year=2020) |
| 2021 | 44 | 76.07 | 14 | [RSF 2021](https://rsf.org/en/index?year=2021) |
| 2022 | 42 | 72.74 | 19 | [RSF 2022](https://rsf.org/en/index?year=2022) |
| 2023 | 45 | 71.22 | 15 | [RSF 2023](https://rsf.org/en/index?year=2023) |
| 2024 | 55 | 66.59 | 14 | [RSF 2024](https://rsf.org/en/index?year=2024) |
| 2025 | 57 | 65.487 | 21 | [RSF 2025](https://rsf.org/en/index?year=2025) |
| 2026 | 64 | 62.61 | 20 | [RSF 2026](https://rsf.org/en/index) |

## What is the World Press Freedom Index?

The World Press Freedom Index is an annual ranking of 180 countries and territories published by Reporters Without Borders, known by its French initials RSF ([glossary: RSF](/glossary/reporters-without-borders)). RSF was "founded in 1985 in Montpellier by four journalists," has its international headquarters in Paris and offices in cities including Washington, D.C. ([RSF, Who are we](https://rsf.org/en/who-are-we)). RSF says the purpose of the index "is to compare the level of freedom enjoyed by journalists and media in 180 countries and territories" ([RSF methodology](https://rsf.org/en/methodology-used-compiling-world-press-freedom-index-2026)).

RSF defines press freedom as "the ability of journalists as individuals and collectives to select, produce, and disseminate news in the public interest independent of political, economic, legal, and social interference and in the absence of threats to their physical and mental safety" ([RSF methodology](https://rsf.org/en/methodology-used-compiling-world-press-freedom-index-2026)). RSF and other press freedom groups treat a free press as a cornerstone of democracy, on the reasoning that citizens cannot hold elected officials to account without independent reporting on what those political actors do in office.

### How is the index calculated?

Each country receives a score from 0 to 100, "with 100 being the best possible score" ([RSF methodology](https://rsf.org/en/methodology-used-compiling-world-press-freedom-index-2026)). The score combines "a quantitative tally of abuses against media and journalists in connection with their work" with "a qualitative analysis," evidence based on answers from press freedom specialists to an RSF questionnaire available in 25 languages. The five indicators are political context, legal framework, economic context, sociocultural context and safety; "all of the subsidiary scores contribute equally to the global score."

The legal indicator measures, among other things, "the degree to which journalists and media are free to work without censorship or judicial sanctions" and "the ability to protect sources" ([RSF methodology](https://rsf.org/en/methodology-used-compiling-world-press-freedom-index-2026)); it also weighs journalists' access to information that authorities hold. The safety indicator combines questions about harm to journalists, including violence against reporters, with RSF's count of abuses in the previous year.

### Which year does each index measure?

"The Index is a snapshot of the situation during the calendar year (January-December) prior to its publication," RSF writes, though data are updated when "the press freedom situation changes dramatically" between the end of that year and publication ([RSF methodology](https://rsf.org/en/methodology-used-compiling-world-press-freedom-index-2026)). The 2026 rank of the United States therefore mainly reflects 2025. The September 2026 deactivation of White House hard passes held by CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters falls after the 2026 index was published ([record](/incidents/2026-white-house-bans-cnn-msnow-politico)).

### Is the index linked to World Press Freedom Day?

World Press Freedom Day, May 3, was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in December 1993, on the anniversary of the Declaration of Windhoek ([United Nations](https://www.un.org/en/observances/press-freedom-day)). The day is a United Nations observance; the index is published by RSF, a non-governmental organization.

## Why did the United States fall in the 2026 index?

RSF's United States profile gives its reasons in its own words. On politics, it writes that since returning to the White House in 2025, President Donald Trump "has censored government data, attempted to dismantle US public broadcasters, weaponized independent government agencies to punish media that criticize his actions, halted aid funding for media freedom internationally, sued disfavored outlets, and applied pressure to install cronies to lead others" ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/country/united-states)).

On the law, RSF writes that "the First Amendment to the US Constitution provides broad protections for the press," but that "the PRESS Act, a federal shield law, failed to pass for a second successive time in 2024," and that "more than a dozen states and communities have proposed or enacted laws" (state and local legislation, rather than federal statute) "to limit journalists' access to public spaces, bar them from legislative meetings, or prevent them from recording the police" ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/country/united-states)). The First Amendment is the part of the United States Constitution that protects freedom of speech and of the press ([glossary](/glossary/first-amendment)).

On safety, RSF cites the U.S. Press Freedom Tracker, a database of press freedom incidents in the United States ([glossary](/glossary/us-press-freedom-tracker)): "there were more than 170 attacks on journalists in 2025, nearly double" the number recorded last year ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/country/united-states)). These figures point to a broader pattern of pressure on local and national newsrooms documented throughout RSF's profile. For example, the PRESS Act is one of the measures meant to protect journalists, since a federal shield law would let reporters refuse to reveal confidential sources in court. On the media economy, RSF cites the Medill Local News Initiative's finding that "as many as 50 million Americans lived in 'news deserts' in 2025," meaning many local media outlets have closed and left communities without dedicated coverage.

### Dated United States actions in 2025

The record documents the following government actions in 2025, each on its own page with sources: on February 25, the White House took over selection of the presidential press pool ([record](/incidents/2025-whca-loses-control-of-press-pool)); on April 25, the Department of Justice rescinded rules limiting subpoenas of journalists ([record](/incidents/2025-doj-rescinds-media-subpoena-guidelines)); on May 1, the president signed Executive Order 14290 directing an end to federal funding for NPR and PBS ([record](/incidents/2025-trump-order-ends-cpb-funding-npr-pbs)); and from October 15, most news organizations turned in their Pentagon press credentials rather than sign new Department of Defense regulations ([record](/incidents/2025-pentagon-press-corps-forfeits-badges)). RSF does not say how much each action weighed in its score.

### What does RSF say about the media economy and society in the United States?

RSF writes that "the US media landscape is relatively diverse, especially online, but ownership of traditional and mainstream media is highly concentrated" among a small number of media outlets, a concentration press freedom groups say weakens editorial independence, and that the president "has tried to pressure these companies to soften their stance on him and install his allies in leadership positions" ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/country/united-states)). On society, it writes that "more Americans have no trust in the media than trust it a fair amount," and adds: "Online harassment, particularly towards women and minorities, is also a serious issue for journalists." It records that "the last journalist to be killed in the course of his work was Dylan Lyons in February of 2023."

## What did the 2026 index find worldwide?

RSF's 2026 analysis states that "for the first time in the history of the Reporters Without Borders (RSF) World Press Freedom Index, over half of the world's countries now fall into the 'difficult' or 'very serious' categories for press freedom" ([RSF, 2026 analysis](https://rsf.org/en/2026-rsf-index-press-freedom-25-year-low)), a decline RSF frames as a global press freedom crisis rather than one confined to the countries in its "very serious" category. It says the legal indicator "has declined the most over the past year, a clear sign that journalism is increasingly criminalised worldwide," and RSF ties that global press freedom slide to weakening democracy in a number of member states of international bodies. RSF attributes part of the decline since 2001 to "the expansion of increasingly restrictive legal arsenals," particularly "those linked to national security policies." RSF's editorial director, Anne Bocandé, said the organization's call "starts with ending the criminalisation of journalism: the misuse of national security laws, SLAPPs, and the systematic obstruction of those who investigate, expose and name names." A SLAPP is a lawsuit filed to burden a journalist or outlet with legal costs ([glossary: SLAPP](/glossary/slapp)).

## Which country has the freest press in the world?

Norway ranks first in the 2026 index, with a score of 92.72, and RSF's global press freedom rankings have placed Nordic democracies at the top for years. RSF writes that "Norway holds the top spot for the tenth consecutive year, while Eritrea comes in last for the third year in a row" ([RSF, 2026 analysis](https://rsf.org/en/2026-rsf-index-press-freedom-25-year-low)); Eritrea and North Korea, both one-party states rather than democracies, anchor the bottom of the index most years.

## What other measures of press freedom exist?

Other organizations publish their own measures, with their own methods, of press freedom and journalism worldwide, and together they sketch a picture of media governance across many legal systems. [Freedom House](/glossary/freedom-house), a United States-based organization founded in 1941, publishes Freedom in the World, an annual assessment of political rights, civil liberties and the health of democracy in each country it covers. The [Committee to Protect Journalists](/glossary/committee-to-protect-journalists), a non-profit in New York, counts journalists imprisoned and killed each year and offers support to those facing threats or restrictions on their work; the committee's tally is one of several benchmarks observers cite alongside RSF's index. The [U.S. Press Freedom Tracker](/glossary/us-press-freedom-tracker) records incidents in the United States. The [tactics index](/tactics) groups government actions by type across countries. RSF publishes the World Press Freedom Index annually, so its next edition will show whether the United States' decline continues, levels off or reverses.
